Cover Page
This is an initial public offering of shares of Class A common stock of Anthropic, PBC. We are selling shares of Class A common stock and the selling stockholders identified in this prospectus are selling an additional shares of Class A common stock. We will not receive any proceeds from the sale of shares of our Class A common stock by any of the selling stockholders. Prior to this offering, there has been no public market for our Class A common stock. It is currently estimated that the initial public offering price per share will be between $ and $ . We have applied to list our Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.” We have a novel capital and corporate governance structure. We are incorporated as a public benefit corporation under Delaware law, a structure consistent with our commitment to artificial intelligence (“AI”) safety and responsibility.

Cover Page
As a public benefit corporation, we are required to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the specific public benefit purpose identified in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation: the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. We created our Long-Term Benefit Trust (the “LTBT”) to help ensure that Anthropic, PBC is managed in a manner that responsibly balances its goals as a public benefit corporation. The LTBT is intended to operate as an independent body of financially disinterested trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise. Through a special class of common stock, Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors.

Cover Page
Our Class T common stock does not otherwise have voting rights with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally and has no economic rights. Immediately prior to the completion of this offering, we will also issue a single share of Class F common stock, a special class of our common stock, to a limited liability company organized by our co-founders (the “Founder LLC”). Dario Amodei, our Chief Executive Officer and a member of our board of directors, and Daniela Amodei, our President and Chairperson of our board of directors, together with our five other co-founders, will initially be the sole members of the Founder LLC. Our Class F common stock, which will be held by the Founder LLC, will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors.

Cover Page
Our Class F common stock will not have any economic rights. Upon the completion of this offering, we will also authorize a special class of our common stock, Class E common stock, which will be issued to our employees, excluding our co-founders. Our Class E common stock will be entitled to vote only on certain limited matters and will not have any economic rights. In addition, we have authorized Class A common stock and Class N common stock. The rights of the holders of Class A common stock and Class N common stock are identical, except with respect to voting and conversion. Each share of Class A common stock is entitled to one vote per share and shares of Class N common stock have no voting rights, except as otherwise required by law. The holders of our Class N common stock are primarily strategic business partners, and shares of Class N common stock will generally convert to Class A common stock upon a sale or transfer to an unaffiliated third party.

Cover Page
Our Class A common stock is not convertible. See the sections titled “Risk Factors—Risks Related to our Governance Structure,” “Our Governance Structure and Its Goals,” and “Description of Capital Stock” for more information. See the sections titled “Our Governance Structure and Its Goals,” “Management,” and “Description of Capital Stock” for additional information. See the section titled “Risk Factors” beginning on page 26 to read about factors you should consider before buying shares of our Class A common stock.

Select Defined Terms
The following are abbreviations, acronyms, and definitions of certain terms used in this prospectus:

Select Defined Terms
This introduces a glossary of technical and financial terms used throughout the filing.

Select Defined Terms
“agent loop” refers to the iterative cycle in which an AI agent receives a task, takes an action, such as planning a project, running code, or calling a tool, observes the result, and decides its next step, with this cycle repeating until the task is complete. The agent loop is the core execution pattern underlying agentic AI behavior.

Select Defined Terms
An agent loop is the repeated cycle in which an AI takes a step, checks the result, and decides what to do next until the task is finished, which is how Claude works through multi-step tasks.

Select Defined Terms
“agentic AI” refers to AI systems that, with varying degrees of autonomy, can plan, determine, and sequence actions and execute them to accomplish defined objectives, including through interaction with external tools, services, datasets, and environments on behalf of a user.

Select Defined Terms
Agentic AI means AI that plans and carries out a series of actions on its own for a user, including using outside tools and services.

Select Defined Terms
“AI” refers to artificial intelligence, a machine-based system that learns or is trained from data and, for explicit or implicit objectives and with varying levels of autonomy, processes that data to infer patterns, generate outputs—such as predictions, content, recommendations, and decisions—and act upon physical or virtual environments.

Select Defined Terms
AI here means a machine system that learns from data to find patterns and produce outputs such as predictions, content, decisions, and actions.

Select Defined Terms
“AI accelerators” refer to processors purpose-built or adapted for the large-scale computations required to pre-train, post-train, refine, and run AI models. These processors are significantly more efficient and faster than general-purpose processors for AI workloads.

Select Defined Terms
AI accelerators are chips built for training and running AI models, which are much faster and more efficient at this work than ordinary processors.

Select Defined Terms
“API” refers to application programming interface, a standardized interface that allows external software to access a system’s capabilities programmatically. AI model providers may offer APIs that allow software developers to send inputs to an AI model and receive outputs, enabling integration into the software developers’ products and workflows.

Select Defined Terms
An API is a way for other companies' software to send requests to Claude and get answers back, letting developers build Claude into their own products.

Select Defined Terms
“Applied AI” refers to a discipline and organizational function focused on embedding AI capabilities directly into production business environments to address specific customer requirements. Applied AI teams, which include forward-deployed engineers, work with enterprises to design and deploy custom solutions, specialized workflows, and domain-specific implementations tailored to a customer’s own systems and processes.

Select Defined Terms
Applied AI is Anthropic's team of engineers who work inside customer companies to build custom Claude setups that fit those customers' systems.

Select Defined Terms
“closing the loop” refers to a development cycle in which successive versions of an AI model assist in building the next, with the goal of compounding capability gains over time.

Select Defined Terms
Closing the loop means using each version of Claude to help build the next one, with the aim of speeding up improvement over time.

Select Defined Terms
“compute” refers to the computational processing resources used to train and run AI models, including, without limitation, specialized AI accelerators, memory, networking, storage, and power systems that are deployed in data centers or other physical computing environments.

Select Defined Terms
Compute means all the physical computing resources used to train and run AI, including specialized chips, memory, networking, storage, and power in data centers.

Select Defined Terms
“compute multipliers” refer to algorithmic and methodological improvements in training and inference that increase the effective output of a given amount of compute.

Select Defined Terms
Compute multipliers are technical improvements that let the same amount of computing hardware produce more useful results.

Select Defined Terms
“computer use” refers to an AI capability that allows a model to observe and interact with a graphical user interface, such as clicking, typing, and navigating applications, similar to how a human operator would.

Select Defined Terms
Computer use is Claude's ability to operate a computer screen the way a person does, by clicking, typing, and moving between applications.

Select Defined Terms
“Constitutional AI” refers to an approach to training AI models using a set of written principles, which we refer to as Claude’s constitution, currently organized around four priorities: being broadly safe, broadly ethical, compliant with our guidelines, and genuinely helpful. Under Constitutional AI, our models evaluate, critique, and revise their own responses against these principles, enabling us to define and control model behavior through auditable principles, rather than relying solely on fixed rule-based instructions or human reviewers.

Select Defined Terms
Constitutional AI is Anthropic's method of training Claude against a written set of principles, prioritizing safety, ethics, Anthropic's guidelines, and helpfulness, so its behavior can be checked against stated rules.

Select Defined Terms
“context window” refers to the maximum amount of text, code, or other content, measured in tokens, that an AI model can process in a given request, encompassing instructions, prior conversation history, user input, and the model’s output.

Select Defined Terms
The context window is the maximum amount of material, counted in tokens, that a model can handle in one request, including instructions, history, input, and its answer.

Select Defined Terms
“CSP” refers to a cloud services provider, a technology company that owns and operates large-scale cloud computing infrastructure and provides on-demand compute, storage, and networking. CSPs may also serve as distribution channels through which AI products and services are made available to customers. The largest CSPs, sometimes referred to as hyperscalers, operate at global scale with significant infrastructure and market concentration.

Select Defined Terms
A CSP is a cloud provider that owns and rents out large data centers, and the biggest ones also act as channels through which customers buy AI products.

Select Defined Terms
“customer” refers to a prosumer or an organization that uses our models, platform, or applications.

Select Defined Terms
A customer means either an individual professional subscriber or an organization that uses Anthropic's models, platform, or applications.

Select Defined Terms
“customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis,” “customers with $1 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis,” and “customers with $10 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis” each refer to customers contributing revenue equal to or greater than the applicable dollar amount during the trailing twelve-month (“TTM”) period ending on the measurement date. For purposes of this metric, we define a customer as a distinct organization, identified by aggregating the accounts that we determine belong to the same organization based on internal records and available data. We do not separately define or internally track a category of “enterprise” customers, and our customers are not segmented or measured internally by reference to whether a given customer is an “enterprise.

Select Defined Terms
” Because spending $100,000 or more on our products is generally characteristic of organizational rather than individual usage, we use the number of and revenue from customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis as our measure of enterprise adoption and engagement with Claude throughout this prospectus, including in references to “enterprise customers” and “enterprise adoption.”

Select Defined Terms
Anthropic counts large customers by spending over the last twelve months at $100,000, $1 million, and $10 million thresholds, and treats those spending $100,000 or more as its measure of business adoption since it does not track an enterprise category.

Select Defined Terms
“frontier AI” refers to AI systems at the current leading edge of capability and safety, performing at or near the highest levels of any existing system across a broad range of tasks.

Select Defined Terms
Frontier AI means the most capable AI systems that exist at a given time, performing at or near the top across many tasks.

Select Defined Terms
“hallucinations” refer to outputs in which an AI model generates factually incorrect or fabricated information with apparent confidence.

Select Defined Terms
Hallucinations are cases where an AI states false or invented information as if it were true.

Select Defined Terms
“inference” refers to the process by which a trained AI model processes an input and generates an output. Inference occurs each time a user or agent interacts with an AI system.

Select Defined Terms
Inference is the work a trained model does each time it answers a request, which is the ongoing computing cost of serving customers.

Select Defined Terms
“interleaved thinking” refers to a capability whereby an AI model interposes discrete reasoning steps between successive tool calls within a single response, rather than confining its reasoning to a single planning phase at the outset.

Select Defined Terms
Interleaved thinking means the model reasons between each tool it uses within one response, rather than planning everything only at the start.

Select Defined Terms
“interpretability” refers to research into how and why AI models produce specific outputs, with the goal of making model behavior more transparent and verifiable, especially in high-stakes applications.

Select Defined Terms
Interpretability is research into why AI models produce the outputs they do, aimed at making their behavior more transparent and checkable.

Select Defined Terms
“knowledge work” refers to complex cognitive work and related professional activities, including obtaining, producing, analyzing, and communicating information through tasks such as coding, drafting analyses, synthesizing research, building financial models, and managing and automating documents and workflows.

Select Defined Terms
Knowledge work means professional thinking tasks such as coding, analysis, research, financial modeling, and handling documents and workflows.

Select Defined Terms
“LLMs” refer to large language models, or AI models trained primarily on large datasets to understand and generate natural language and computer code.

Select Defined Terms
LLMs, or large language models, are AI models trained on huge amounts of text and code to understand and produce language and software.

Select Defined Terms
“mechanistic interpretability” refers to a subfield of interpretability research focused on reverseengineering the internal computations of neural networks. Rather than inferring model behavior from inputs and outputs alone, mechanistic interpretability seeks to identify the specific features and circuits within a model that give rise to its behavior with the goal of making model reasoning auditable at the mechanism level and detecting failure modes, including deceptive or unsafe behavior, that may not surface in standard testing.

Select Defined Terms
Mechanistic interpretability tries to map the internal workings of a model to see what causes its behavior, including spotting deceptive or unsafe behavior that ordinary testing might miss.

Select Defined Terms
“model weights” refer to the numerical parameters encoding a trained AI model’s behavior, which are the primary intellectual asset of a frontier AI developer, representing the accumulated investment in compute, data, and research.

Select Defined Terms
Model weights are the numbers that make up a trained model and are a frontier AI company's most valuable asset, representing its spending on computing, data, and research.

Select Defined Terms
“multi-agent orchestration” refers to an architecture in which multiple AI agents collaborate on a shared task, with one coordinating while others execute subtasks in parallel, enabling more complex, long-horizon work than a single agent can complete alone.

Select Defined Terms
Multi-agent orchestration is a setup where one AI agent coordinates several others working on parts of a task at once, allowing longer and more complex work.

Select Defined Terms
“Net Revenue Retention” reflects customer expansion, contraction, and churn as of a measurement date. We calculate Net Revenue Retention by dividing the Qualified Customers’ Current Period revenue by their Base Period revenue. A Qualified Customer is a customer with at least $1 of revenue during the Base Period, excluding subscribers to our Claude Pro and Max plans, whose fixed-price subscriptions do not reflect the expansion and contraction behavior this metric is intended to capture. The Base Period is the three months ending a year prior to the measurement date. The Current Period is the three months ending as of the measurement date.

Select Defined Terms
Net Revenue Retention compares what a group of existing customers paid in the latest three months with what they paid in the same three months a year earlier, excluding Claude Pro and Max subscribers, showing whether existing customers spend more or less.

Select Defined Terms
“open-weight” refers to an AI model whose trained model weights, or the numerical parameters encoding the model’s learned behavior, are publicly released, allowing third parties to download, run, and modify the model, subject to the terms of the model’s license, without necessarily providing access to the underlying training data or code.

Select Defined Terms
An open-weight model is one whose weights are published so anyone can download, run, and modify it, which makes it a potential free or cheap alternative to Anthropic's paid models.

Select Defined Terms
“pay-for-intelligence” or “consumption” refers to our revenue model under which customers pay for their usage of our intelligence service, which is metered in tokens and priced according to the model selected.

Select Defined Terms
Pay-for-intelligence, or consumption, is Anthropic's pricing model in which customers pay for how much they use, measured in tokens and priced by which model they choose.

Select Defined Terms
“persistent,” in the context of AI applications, refers to denoting data, state, or context that is continuously retained beyond the boundary of a single operation, session, or interaction, remaining accessible for reuse across subsequent steps, sessions, or workflows without requiring reinitialization.

Select Defined Terms
Persistent means information or context that an AI application keeps across steps and sessions so it does not have to start over each time.

Select Defined Terms
“post-training” refers to the collection of techniques applied to a pre-trained model to refine its behavior, including reinforcement learning, supervised refinement methods, and other alignment methods. Post-training is the stage in which much of the work to make a frontier model helpful, accurate, and safe is performed, including the application of safety and alignment techniques.

Select Defined Terms
Post-training is the stage after initial training where a model is refined to be helpful, accurate, and safe, including through reinforcement learning and safety methods.

Select Defined Terms
“pre-training” refers to the initial stage of training an AI model, in which the model learns general patterns and representations from large-scale datasets of text, code, and other data, typically by predicting the next token in a sequence. The output of pre-training is a base model with broad capabilities that has not yet been adapted for any specific deployment context.

Select Defined Terms
Pre-training is the first, large-scale stage of building a model, where it learns general patterns from massive amounts of text, code, and other data.

Select Defined Terms
“primitives” refer to the foundational, modular building blocks of a software system from which more complex applications and workflows are constructed.

Select Defined Terms
Primitives are basic building blocks of software from which more complex applications are assembled.

Select Defined Terms
“prompt injection” refers to an adversarial technique in which malicious instructions are embedded in content an AI model is asked to process, such as websites, documents, or tool outputs, with the aim of overriding or manipulating the model’s intended behavior, typically without the user’s knowledge.

Select Defined Terms
Prompt injection is an attack in which hidden instructions are planted in a website, document, or tool output to hijack what the AI does, usually without the user knowing.

Select Defined Terms
“prosumers” refer to individual users who subscribe to AI tools to perform knowledge work.

Select Defined Terms
Prosumers are individual people who pay for AI tools to do professional work.

Select Defined Terms
“reinforcement learning” refers to a machine learning approach in which a model learns to perform a task by taking actions, receiving feedback signals called rewards, and adjusting its behavior to maximize the rewards it accrues over time. In contemporary AI development, reinforcement learning is widely used to refine model behavior after pre-training, including to improve helpfulness, accuracy, and adherence to safety guidelines.

Select Defined Terms
Reinforcement learning trains a model by rewarding good actions so it learns to repeat them, and it is widely used after pre-training to improve helpfulness, accuracy, and safety.

Select Defined Terms
“RLHF” refers to reinforcement learning from human feedback, a specific form of reinforcement learning in which human evaluators rate the model’s responses, and those ratings are used as the reward signal to guide training.

Select Defined Terms
RLHF is reinforcement learning in which human reviewers score the model's answers and those scores guide its training.

Select Defined Terms
“Run-Rate Revenue” is an operating metric that refers to the estimated annualized value of our revenuegenerating activity as of a measurement date, calculated as the sum of (i) our consumption-based fees during the trailing 28-day period ended on the measurement date, multiplied by 13, and (ii) our aggregate monthly subscription fees as of the measurement date, multiplied by 12. For purposes of calculating Run-Rate Revenue, consumption-based fees and subscription-based fees are derived from customer usage and active subscriptions.

Select Defined Terms
Run-Rate Revenue is an annualized estimate that multiplies the last 28 days of usage fees by 13 and current monthly subscriptions by 12, so it reflects current momentum rather than revenue actually earned over a year.

Select Defined Terms
“SIs” refer to systems integrators, or third-party technology and professional services firms that design, build, and deploy integrated solutions for customers by combining products and services from multiple technology vendors into unified systems tailored to customer needs.

Select Defined Terms
SIs, or systems integrators, are consulting and technology firms that combine products from several vendors into finished systems for customers.

Select Defined Terms
“tokens” refer to numeric units into which an AI model converts the data it processes, including text, images, audio, and video, the number of which varies by the model and tokenizer applied. Tokens are the smallest individual units of a language model and can correspond to words, subwords, characters, or bytes. A tokenizer is the component of a model that converts customer inputs into the sequence of tokens the model processes and then converts the processed tokens into the outputs provided to customers.

Select Defined Terms
Tokens are the small units, such as word pieces or characters, that a model breaks data into, and they are the unit Anthropic uses to meter and charge for usage.

This summary highlights selected information that is presented in greater detail elsewhere in this prospectus. This summary does not contain all of the information you should consider before investing in our Class A common stock. You should read this entire prospectus carefully, including the sections titled “Risk Factors,” “Special Note Regarding Forward-looking Statements,” “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations,” “Business,” and “Our Governance Structure and Its Goals,” as well as our consolidated financial statements and the related notes included elsewhere in this prospectus, before making an investment decision.

Prospectus Summary
Unless the context otherwise requires, the terms “Anthropic,” “the company,” “we,” “us,” and “our” in this prospectus refer to Anthropic, PBC and its consolidated subsidiaries, and references to our “common stock” refer to our Class A common stock, Class N common stock, and Class F common stock (and, where the context requires, our Class T common stock and our Class E common stock).

Prospectus Summary
The summary covers only highlights, and Anthropic says investors should read the full prospectus, especially the risk factors, financial discussion, and governance sections, before deciding to invest.

Overview
For the first time in history, intelligence is something humans can build. The cognitive capability to reason, analyze, synthesize, decide, and create is producible at scale and accessible on demand. We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet. AI that truly delivers on its potential—with the risks well managed—could significantly accelerate global growth and dramatically improve quality of life for people around the world.

Overview
Anthropic argues that AI makes intelligence something that can be produced at scale and predicts it will transform the economy more than industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, or the internet, if its risks are managed.

Overview
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a team of researchers responsible for many of the breakthroughs that define AI. We are first and foremost a research lab—our mission is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. This mission directs our focus—along with our talent and culture, our frontier and safety research, our approach to compute, and our enterprise strategy, it is one of the core advantages that set us apart. These advantages enable us to continuously advance frontier AI and shape the standards for its safe and responsible development. Our frontier AI, Claude, is delivered to customers through our models, platform, and applications. Claude has experienced the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, as demonstrated by revenue growing from $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $ for the three months ended September 30, 2026.

Overview
This rapid and growing adoption generates two self-reinforcing dynamics—an improvement loop that advances Claude and an investment loop that helps fund our continued research in frontier AI.

Overview
Anthropic, founded in 2021, calls itself a research lab with a safety mission and says Claude's revenue grew from $0 at its early 2023 launch to an amount still blank for the three months ended September 30, 2026.

Our Core Advantages
Mission & Focus. All of our efforts are guided by a singular focus on our mission. This focus enables us to concentrate talent, research, and compute investment on the highest-value work for humanity and to avoid conflicting priorities. Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while mitigating the most significant risks, and we believe this requires safety and capability to advance together.

Our Core Advantages
Anthropic says its mission keeps it focused on the most valuable work and that it believes safety and capability must advance together.

Our Core Advantages
Talent & Culture. Our mission and focus enable us to attract and retain world-class talent, including researchers and engineers who want their work to shape a better future. We also have a culture that promotes a low-ego, truth-seeking environment, where frontier AI capability and safety are mutually reinforcing. The Importance of Safety and Ethical Behavior
While the potential benefits of AI are extraordinary, its rapid advancement will impact the economy and society in ways that could create significant disruption, particularly if the technology is not developed and deployed responsibly. For example, bad actors have already conducted high-profile cyberattacks using AI’s capabilities to discover vulnerabilities, generate malware, and evade detection tools; other risks associated with misuse, including in the domain of biology, could result in even greater harm. AI deployed at scale also has the potential to concentrate power and wealth both within and between countries in ways that could erode trust, harm society, and destabilize the geopolitical order. Misaligned AI systems could corrupt institutional decisionmaking or cause large-scale harm through autonomous actions that are not visible or understandable to their users and operators.

The Importance of Safety and Ethical Behavior
We believe that frontier AI companies must invest in safety and alignment to help ensure the responsible diffusion of this technology. We also believe that safety, alignment, and ethical behavior resonate particularly strongly with enterprises, where rigorous safeguards, predictable model behavior, and demonstrable accountability have become decisive criteria in selecting an AI partner for mission-critical workloads.

The Importance of Safety and Ethical Behavior
Anthropic warns AI is already being used in cyberattacks and could enable biological harm, concentrate power, or act in hidden harmful ways, and argues that safety investment both reduces these risks and wins business customers.

Claude as a Virtual Collaborator
Claude Code. The clearest manifestation of Virtual Collaborators today is Claude Code, our coding agent and the product we believe has most concretely defined what autonomous AI work looks like. Claude Code shifted the market’s understanding of what an AI system could do in collaboration with software developers: the model suggests the next line of code and goes further by planning, writing, testing, and debugging—a process that results in production-grade code. Within months of its release, autonomous coding became the reference point for measuring the progress of frontier AI. For enterprise AI use cases, we believe the launch of Claude Code was comparable in its impact to the introduction of the first widely adopted conversational AI assistants.

Claude as a Virtual Collaborator
What makes Claude Code a Virtual Collaborator is its sustained reasoning, a harness that translates intent into actions, an execution environment that maintains a persistent state whether on a developer’s machine or in a sandboxed cloud environment, integration with existing tools and systems, and a user-friendly interface. Its uses are highly varied and often surprising: for example, NASA engineers used Claude Code to plan and write navigation commands for the Mars Perseverance rover, resulting in the first AI-planned drive on Mars.

Our Governance Structure and Its Goals
Our novel capital and corporate governance structure has been carefully designed and differs significantly from that of other public companies. We strive to help bring humanity safely into an era where transformative AI exerts tremendous and potentially decisive influence over a broad range of human undertakings. Operating as a public benefit corporation (“PBC”) gives our board of directors the necessary latitude to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the specific public benefit purpose that we promote. Our specific public benefit purpose is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity (the “Company Purpose”).

Our Governance Structure and Its Goals
In addition, a financially disinterested trust, which we refer to as the Long-Term Benefit Trust (the “LTBT”) and which generally has the power to elect and remove a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors, is designed to supply both the incentives and insights for striking this balance appropriately. We also believe that our seven co-founders are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission.

Our Governance Structure and Its Goals
Anthropic's governance is unusual for a public company: as a public benefit corporation its board weighs profit against societal effects and its mission, and an independent trust picks most directors.

Public Benefit Corporation Status
Consistent with our long-term commitment to AI safety and responsibility, we are incorporated as a PBC under Delaware law. PBCs are a class of corporations that are intended to produce a public benefit and operate in a responsible and sustainable manner. Under Delaware law, a PBC is required to identify in its certificate of incorporation the public benefit or benefits it will promote, and its directors have a duty to manage the affairs of the corporation in a manner that balances the pecuniary interests of the corporation’s stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by the corporation’s conduct, and the specific public benefit purpose identified in the corporation’s certificate of incorporation. As provided in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, the public benefit that we promote, which we must always consider in the management of our company, is the Company Purpose.

Public Benefit Corporation Status
Under Delaware law, Anthropic as a public benefit corporation must balance shareholder financial interests, the interests of people affected by its conduct, and its stated purpose of developing advanced AI responsibly for humanity's long-term benefit.

Long-Term Benefit Trust
In 2023, we implemented an innovative governance structure featuring the LTBT, which is designed to ensure that we are managed in a manner that responsibly balances our tripartite goals as a PBC: the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose. The LTBT is intended to operate as an independent body of five financially disinterested voting trustees (“Trustees”) with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise. Through a special class of common stock, Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Our Class T common stock does not otherwise have voting rights on matters submitted to stockholders generally.

Long-Term Benefit Trust
Since 2023, the Long-Term Benefit Trust, five trustees with no financial stake, has held a special Class T stock that lets it elect and remove a majority of Anthropic's board, though that stock has no other voting rights.

Risk Factors Summary
• Our success depends in large part on our ability to continue to develop the most advanced and capable AI models, and any failure to do so could adversely affect our business.

Anthropic's business depends on continuing to build the most advanced AI models, and falling behind would hurt it.

Risk Factors Summary
• Constraints on the critical inputs supporting compute could limit our ability to secure adequate compute.

Shortages of the inputs behind compute, such as chips or power, could limit how much computing capacity Anthropic can obtain.

Risk Factors Summary
• We are highly dependent on the continued service of our co-founders, senior management team, and key technical employees, and the loss of any of these individuals may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

Risk Factors Summary
Losing co-founders, senior leaders or key technical staff could hurt Anthropic's business.

Risk Factors Summary
• Our company culture has contributed to our success and, if we cannot maintain this culture as we grow, our business could be adversely affected.

Risk Factors Summary
Anthropic credits its culture for its success and warns that losing it while growing could harm the business.

Risk Factors Summary
• We face intense competition, and if we are unable to compete effectively, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.

Risk Factors Summary
Anthropic faces intense competition, and failing to keep up could hurt its results.

Risk Factors Summary
• If the market for our models, platform, and applications develops more slowly than we expect or declines, our growth may slow or stall, and our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.

Risk Factors Summary
If demand for Anthropic's AI grows more slowly than expected or shrinks, its growth could slow or stop.

Risk Factors Summary
• If the use of our AI models results in harm, whether through use by malicious actors or misuse by other third parties, or if our model guardrails or safeguards fail to prevent such misuse, our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.

Risk Factors Summary
If people misuse Claude to cause harm, or its safeguards fail, Anthropic's reputation and finances could suffer.

Risk Factors Summary
• Our AI models may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed, which could adversely affect our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations.

Risk Factors Summary
Claude itself could act in unintended or harmful ways nobody asked for, which could damage Anthropic's reputation and business.

Risk Factors Summary
• We may be exposed to liability, litigation, and regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models, and our contractual protections and insurance may be insufficient, any of which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

Risk Factors Summary
Harms linked to Claude could lead to lawsuits and regulatory action, and Anthropic's contracts and insurance may not fully cover the costs.

Risk Factors Summary
• A substantial portion of our revenue and accounts receivable is driven by a limited number of customers and distribution channels, and the loss of, or a significant reduction in, spend from one or more of our top customers or disruption through those channels could adversely affect our prospects, business, and financial condition.

Risk Factors Summary
A large share of Anthropic's revenue comes from a few customers and sales channels, so losing one or seeing it cut spending could hurt results significantly.

Risk Factors Summary
• We have a limited operating history in an evolving and nascent industry, which makes it difficult to evaluate our future prospects and may increase the risk that we will not be successful.

Risk Factors Summary
Anthropic has a short track record in a young, fast-changing industry, which makes its future hard to judge.

Risk Factors Summary
• We are at an early stage of our revenue growth, we have experienced rapid growth in recent periods, and our historical growth rates are not indicative of future performance or our ability to sustain or forecast future revenue growth.

Risk Factors Summary
Anthropic's recent very rapid growth does not mean it will continue, and future revenue is hard to forecast.

Risk Factors Summary
• Our business is subject to an evolving and uncertain regulatory and political environment, which could increase our costs, restrict our operations, or adversely affect demand for our models, platform, and applications.

Risk Factors Summary
Changing laws and politics around AI could raise Anthropic's costs, restrict its operations or reduce demand.

Risk Factors Summary
• Our reliance on a limited number of CSPs and suppliers, some of which have strategic and investment relationships with us and are our customers, creates complex dynamics that could give rise to conflicts of interest and adversely affect our access to compute.

Risk Factors Summary
Anthropic relies on a few cloud providers and suppliers that are also its investors and customers, creating potential conflicts of interest that could affect its access to compute.

Risk Factors Summary
• Our capital stock structure features certain provisions that are novel or otherwise not common among other corporations with multiple-class structures, and may effectively eliminate the ability of holders of our Class A common stock to influence important decisions, including a change in control.

Risk Factors Summary
Anthropic's unusual share structure may leave ordinary Class A shareholders with essentially no say over major decisions, including a sale of the company.

Risk Factors Summary
• Our capital structure will concentrate voting power with the LTBT and the Founder LLC for the foreseeable future and will result in the LTBT and the Founder LLC having voting power that is not derived from or proportionate to economic interests in our company.

The trust and the Founder LLC will hold voting control for the foreseeable future, far out of proportion to their economic ownership.

Risk Factors Summary
• Our focus on the long-term best interests of our company as a PBC, and the duty of our directors to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those stakeholders materially affected by our conduct, and our Company Purpose, may conflict with short-, medium-, or long-term financial interests and business performance, which may negatively impact the value of our Class A common stock.

Because directors must weigh the public and the mission alongside shareholder returns, decisions may sometimes hurt financial performance and the Class A share price.

The development, deployment, and use of AI technologies are subject to rapidly evolving and increasingly complex laws, regulations, and governmental scrutiny across multiple jurisdictions. Governments and regulatory authorities in the United States and in other countries in which we operate or distribute our models, platform, and applications have proposed, enacted, or are considering legislation, regulations, and guidance relating to AI model development and deployment, data usage and privacy, transparency, safety, consumer protection, content generation, intellectual property, cybersecurity, export controls, and competition.

For example, the EU AI Regulation 2024/1689 (“EU AI Act”), which came into force in August 2024 and will become fully applicable following a transitional period, imposes a range of obligations on AI systems and general-purpose AI models placed on the market or put into service in the EU, including transparency, risk management, and governance requirements, and provides for significant penalties for non-compliance. The application of certain copyright law doctrines and contractual interpretations of opensource licenses to modern AI model training are uncertain.
The application of certain copyright law doctrines and contractual interpretations of open-source licenses to modern AI model training has not been authoritatively resolved by U.S. and non-U.S. courts as of this date. We have a good faith belief that we own or possess all sufficient legal rights and/or defenses to the training data used in or with our AI models, platform, and applications, which is based in part on our belief that our use or acquisition of the training data used in or with our AI models, platform, and applications constitutes “fair use” of such training data under copyright law doctrine. In addition, copyright laws in some jurisdictions outside the United States generally do not recognize fair use, and our reliance on analogous exceptions is subject to evolving conditions and to adverse or unsettled judicial interpretation in those jurisdictions.

The application of certain copyright law doctrines and contractual interpretations of opensource licenses to modern AI model training are uncertain.

In particular, adverse rulings in litigation involving other AI developers, regardless of the specific facts, data practices, or legal theories at issue in those cases, could establish legal precedents or interpretations of copyright law that apply broadly across the industry and limit our ability to train, develop, or deploy AI models, even if our own data procurement and usage practices differ. In general, under Sections 382 and 383 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended (the “Code”), a corporation that undergoes an “ownership change” is subject to annual limitations on its ability to utilize its pre-change U.S. federal NOL carryforwards and certain other tax attributes, including tax credit carryforwards, to offset its future taxable income or tax liabilities. For these purposes, an ownership change generally occurs if the percentage of a corporation’s stock (by value) owned by one or more “5-percent shareholders” increases by more than 50 percentage points over a rolling three-year period. Certain estimates in this prospectus regarding global knowledge workers’ wages, which we refer to as the annual economic value represented by global knowledge workers, are our own, derived from third-party data. Based on wage data for U.S. workers by occupation classification from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics in 2025, we calculate the total salary for the subset of workers that we believe to represent knowledge workers. Based on International Labor Organization data for global labor income as a percentage of global GDP, and based on 2025 global GDP, we estimate a 2025 global wages figure. We calculate the ratio of total U.S. wages in 2025 to the 2025 global wages figure, and apply that ratio to the total U.S. knowledge workers’ wages figure to arrive at an estimate of global knowledge workers’ wages.

Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
This opens management's own explanation of the financial results, warning that it contains forward-looking predictions that may prove wrong and that past results from 2023 through 2025 do not guarantee future performance.

Overview
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a team of researchers responsible for many of the breakthroughs that define AI. We are first and foremost a research lab—our mission is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. This mission directs our focus—along with our talent and culture, our frontier and safety research, our approach to compute, and our enterprise strategy, it is one of the core advantages that set us apart. These advantages enable us to continuously advance frontier AI and shape the standards for its safe and responsible development. Our frontier AI, Claude, is delivered to customers through our models, platform, and applications. Claude has experienced the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, as demonstrated by revenue growing from $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $ for the three months ended September 30, 2026.

Overview
Anthropic describes itself as a research lab founded in 2021 with a mission of developing advanced AI safely for humanity's long-term benefit, and says Claude's revenue grew from $0 at launch in early 2023 to an undisclosed figure for the quarter ended September 30, 2026.

Our Financial Model
Our financial model is built on four primary drivers that define the trajectory of our results:

Our Financial Model
Anthropic says four main factors drive its financial results, listed below.

Our Financial Model
• Adoption of Claude. The advancing intelligence and capabilities of each successive version of a Claude model drive the diffusion of Claude across the global economy. As new customers adopt Claude and existing customers expand their usage into new workflows, our revenue grows.

Our Financial Model
The first factor is customer uptake: each more capable Claude model attracts new customers and leads existing ones to use it for more tasks, which raises revenue.

Our Financial Model
• Compute Efficiency. We are focused on increasing the intelligence produced and revenue generated per dollar of compute invested and have delivered significant efficiency improvements.

Our Financial Model
The second factor is getting more model capability and revenue from each dollar spent on compute, the specialized chips in data centers that train and run Claude, where Anthropic says it has already improved substantially.

Our Financial Model
• Operating Efficiency. Our high talent density, efficient go-to-market, and how extensively our teams leverage Claude in their work help to drive improved operating margin, Adjusted Operating Margin, and revenue per employee.

Our Financial Model
The third factor is running the company lean, with skilled staff, efficient selling and heavy internal use of Claude, which Anthropic says lifts profit margins and revenue per employee.

Our Financial Model
• Compute Investments. Investing in compute is critical to support our long-term growth, and we intend to continue making substantial investments in compute.

Our Financial Model
The fourth factor is continued heavy spending on compute, which Anthropic considers essential for long-term growth and plans to keep doing.

Our Financial Model
The drivers of our financial model materialize on different timelines. The adoption of Claude and associated revenue growth, compute efficiency, and operating efficiency have each increased rapidly over time. Compute is procured and committed in advance and the expense is incurred as it is brought online and added to our fungible pool, often in large, discrete steps. The fungible pool can support all workloads dynamically, including research, model development, serving customers, and internal usage of Claude. As a result, there is a lag between when investment is committed and when the full revenue associated with such investment is realized.

Our Financial Model
Revenue and efficiency rise steadily, but compute costs arrive in large chunks when new capacity comes online, so spending is booked well before the revenue that capacity eventually brings in.

Our Financial Model
This dynamic has produced a financial model in which our operating margin and Adjusted Operating Margin for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 have expanded significantly year over year. As significant incremental compute is brought online in future periods, the associated expense will be recognized in advance of the full revenue that the compute will ultimately support, and we expect operating margin and Adjusted Operating Margin may compress in those periods. At our current stage, this cycle is an inherent aspect of our business and will cause operating margins to fluctuate from period to period, at times meaningfully, even if the underlying economics of the business continue to improve.

Our Financial Model
Operating margins expanded sharply in the nine months ended September 30, 2026, but Anthropic expects them to shrink, sometimes significantly, whenever large new compute arrives, so profits will swing from period to period.

Our Financial Model
In addition, the majority of our compute is contracted under multi-year commitments that we typically procure 12 to 18 months in advance of availability. When customer demand or research needs exceed this long-term capacity, we procure short-term compute, which typically carries a higher cost per unit of compute. We expect our use of short-term compute to increase in the near term and to in turn compress our operating margin and Adjusted Operating Margin as a result.

Our Financial Model
Most compute is reserved 12 to 18 months ahead under multi-year contracts, and when demand outruns it Anthropic buys pricier short-term capacity; it expects to do more of this soon, which will squeeze margins.

Adoption of Claude
Each successive version of a Claude model is designed to advance the frontier with capabilities that customers value most, including coding, agentic workflows, computer use, and complex reasoning, which unlock new categories of use and drive compounding demand from new and existing customers. Claude’s intelligence is a primary driver of its diffusion and our revenue growth: because Claude leads at the AI frontier, customers rapidly adopt it, quickly see real value, and organically expand their use. We complement this intelligence-led growth with direct go-to-market and Applied AI teams and extend our reach through native availability across all three major cloud platforms—AWS, GCP, and Azure—and through partnerships with SIs, consultants, and data platforms.

Adoption of Claude
Anthropic says each Claude model is built to lead on coding, autonomous task handling, computer use and reasoning, which drives demand, and it sells through its own teams, Amazon, Google and Microsoft clouds, and consulting and data partners.

Adoption of Claude
We deliver this intelligence through an integrated approach. Our Claude model family is the foundation, with model classes optimized for different points along the capability-cost-speed curve. On top of our models, Claude Platform gives developers access to the primitives we use ourselves, which they can use to build their own AI solutions. We have also built first-party applications on Claude Platform for customers that prefer a ready-todeploy option. We believe the value of this integrated approach is reflected in the increasing number of customers that use both Claude Platform and our first-party applications. For the three months ended September 30, 2026, over 50% of our customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis used Claude Platform and at least one of our first-party applications, up from approximately 30% for the three months ended December 31, 2025.

Adoption of Claude
Anthropic sells models at different price and speed levels, a developer platform and ready-made apps, and over 50% of its customers paying $100,000 or more yearly used both platform and apps in the September 2026 quarter, up from about 30% in December 2025.

Adoption of Claude
As more customers adopt Claude and expand their usage, we have rapidly grown our base of customers that generate meaningful revenue. We had more than 11,900 customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis as of September 30, 2026, up from more than 950 as of September 30, 2025. In addition, as customers further embed Claude into their most critical workflows and growth initiatives, many rapidly expand their deployments into higher revenue tiers. As of September 30, 2026, we had more than 1,900 customers with $1 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis and approximately 250 customers with $10 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis.

Adoption of Claude
Customers paying $100,000 or more over the past twelve months rose from more than 950 at September 30, 2025 to more than 11,900 a year later, with more than 1,900 above $1 million and about 250 above $10 million.

Adoption of Claude
This customer momentum is driven by significant usage expansion as customers realize the value of deploying Claude across their organizations. The value that Claude delivers to customers has helped drive our Net Revenue Retention of approximately 900% as of September 30, 2026.

Adoption of Claude
Net Revenue Retention of about 900% at September 30, 2026 means existing customers, taken as a group, are spending roughly nine times what they spent a year earlier.

Adoption of Claude
The growth in our business reflects the degree to which enterprises are embedding Claude directly into their business-critical workflows. Despite these trends, adoption across the global economy remains nascent. As Claude’s capabilities continue to advance, we believe the addressable opportunity will expand, and Claude will continue its rapid diffusion across more enterprises.

Adoption of Claude
Anthropic says businesses are building Claude into core operations, yet AI adoption across the economy is still early, and it expects its market to grow as Claude improves.

Compute Efficiency
Compute is the most significant operating cost in our business, and compute efficiency is a critical determinant of our operating efficiency and revenue. Our research-driven algorithmic improvements in training and inference optimization and multi-chip compute architecture have combined to dramatically increase our compute efficiency as our revenue has scaled. The result is that we are able to continue increasing the intelligence our research can produce and the revenue our business can generate per dollar of compute investment.

Compute Efficiency
Paying for compute, meaning the specialized chips in data centers that train and run Claude, is Anthropic's largest operating cost, and the company says it now gets more model capability and more revenue out of each dollar spent on it than before.

Compute Efficiency
We define compute efficiency as maximizing the intelligence produced and revenue generated per dollar of compute invested. Three pillars drive our compute efficiency:

Compute Efficiency
Anthropic defines compute efficiency as getting the most intelligence and revenue per dollar of chips and data centers, and names three areas that drive it, listed next.

Compute Efficiency
• Training Efficiency. Our researchers regularly innovate compute multipliers. Increasingly, Claude itself assists in the research and engineering that produce each successive version of our models, which is a recursive dynamic we refer to as “closing the loop,” with successive versions of our models accelerating the development of the next and compounding these gains across model generations.

Compute Efficiency
Anthropic's researchers keep finding ways to train models with less compute, and Claude itself now helps build the next Claude, which the company calls "closing the loop" and expects to compound across model generations.

Compute Efficiency
• Inference Efficiency. Our researchers have delivered meaningful compute multipliers for inference —reducing the compute required to serve a given level of model performance—while our engineering teams have driven significant optimizations in how efficiently that compute is utilized in production. This allows us to provide greater value for customers and generate greater revenue from our compute base over time, which is critical as we have consistently operated in a compute-constrained environment where customer demand exceeds available compute.

Compute Efficiency
Anthropic has cut the compute needed to run its models for customers at a given quality, which matters because demand has consistently exceeded the compute it has, so each saving lets it serve more customers and earn more.

Compute Efficiency
• Multi-Chip Compute Approach. We train and serve Claude natively across four major chip families (AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs) using a proprietary orchestration layer that enables us to optimize workloads for price and performance. This flexibility, which took years and significant investment to build and we believe is difficult to replicate at scale, expands our available compute, reduces dependence on any single vendor, and enables us to continuously route workloads to the most optimal hardware for those workloads. This foundation, paired with Claude’s increasing understanding of chip and model architectures, allows us to onboard new chip platforms in a fraction of the time this once required.

Compute Efficiency
Anthropic runs Claude on four chip families from Amazon, Google, NVIDIA and AMD using its own software to shift work to the cheapest suitable hardware, which reduces reliance on any one supplier and, it believes, is hard for rivals to copy.

Compute Efficiency
Revenue per dollar of compute has expanded meaningfully, even as we have accelerated research and product velocity and expanded our internal Claude usage. For example, our revenue grew 1,368% year over year for the three months ended June 30, 2026, compared to our compute and infrastructure expenses that grew 300% during the same period. While serving our growing customer demand, we also made significant research advances to the frontier with new leading models, including Mythos 5, Fable 5, and Opus 5, and launched new products, including Claude Cowork and Claude Design.

Compute Efficiency
Anthropic's revenue grew 1,368% year over year in the three months ended June 30, 2026, while compute and infrastructure costs grew 300%, and it has already released models including Mythos 5, Fable 5 and Opus 5 and products including Claude Cowork and Claude Design.

Operating Efficiency
Our operating efficiency is derived from our high talent density, our efficient go-to-market, and how extensively our teams leverage Claude in their work. Claude is the common thread, amplifying the output of our employees. For example, over 90% of the contributions to our codebase in September 2026 were written by Claude. Additionally, the average daily volume of code contributed to our codebase per engineer in the three months ended September 30, 2026 was over 45 times the average daily volume in the year ended December 31, 2024.

Operating Efficiency
Anthropic says Claude itself boosts staff productivity: over 90% of code changes in September 2026 were written by Claude, and code per engineer per day in the September 2026 quarter was over 45 times the 2024 average.

Operating Efficiency
From September 30, 2025 to September 30, 2026, TTM revenue increased approximately 1,200% while headcount increased approximately 170%, driving TTM revenue per employee from $1.4 million to over $6.6 million, a reflection of extraordinary talent density and a culture built to compound it.

Operating Efficiency
Over the year to September 30, 2026, twelve-month revenue grew about 1,200% while staff grew about 170%, lifting revenue per employee from $1.4 million to over $6.6 million.

Operating Efficiency

How We Generate Revenue
At the foundation of our business is our family of four Claude model classes—Mythos (including Fable), Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku—each optimized for a different point on the capability-cost-speed curve. Our frontier models allow customers to match the right model to each use case. Customers typically use higher-capability models for complex reasoning, coding, and agentic workflows where greater model intelligence is required. Customers also frequently adopt our full range of models, routing individual tasks to the models that are most optimized to meet their needs along the capability-cost-speed curve. The model a customer uses and the volume of usage are the primary drivers of customer spend. We establish a direct contractual relationship with the customer and offer customers the flexibility to purchase directly from us or through CSP marketplaces, and many customers utilize both channels.

These dynamics are inherent aspects of a pay-for-intelligence revenue model and may be important determinants of our financial results in future periods.

Compute and Infrastructure
Customers adopt and retain our technology based on whether our models are at the frontier of AI capability and maintaining that frontier position is essential to revenue generation. Each model release represents continuous intelligence improvements, making ongoing model development a critical factor in revenue generation. We operate an iterative cycle in which compute deployed to model development yields more capable and efficient models. Those efficiency gains free compute to serve additional customer workloads. In turn, serving our customers at scale generates feedback that informs research and model development. In this cycle, customerserving activity and model development are each a direct input that informs the other, and we therefore view compute and infrastructure costs as critical to our ability to generate revenue within a short time of incurring such costs.

Anthropic argues compute for research and compute for serving customers feed each other: better models need less compute per customer, and customer use guides research. So it treats all compute spending as directly tied to earning revenue soon after.

Non-GAAP Financial Measures
To supplement our consolidated financial statements prepared and presented in accordance with GAAP, we use certain non-GAAP financial measures, as described below, to facilitate analysis of our operating performance and for internal planning and forecasting purposes.

Non-GAAP Financial Measures
Alongside results under standard US accounting rules (GAAP), Anthropic reports adjusted figures of its own design, which it uses to analyze performance and to plan and forecast.

Non-GAAP Financial Measures
We use Adjusted Operating Income (Loss), Adjusted Operating Margin, and Adjusted Net Income (Loss) to evaluate our operating performance, formulate business plans, prepare budgets and forecasts, and make strategic decisions, including those relating to operating expenses and the allocation of internal resources. By excluding certain items that management believes are not directly reflective of the ongoing operating performance of our business, we believe these non-GAAP financial measures provide investors, analysts, and others with meaningful insight and enhance their overall understanding of our business and financial performance by providing a more consistent and comparable overview of our financial performance across periods.

Non-GAAP Financial Measures
Management uses three adjusted measures for budgets, forecasts and resource decisions, and argues that removing certain items gives a more consistent view of the business from one period to the next.

Non-GAAP Financial Measures
Other companies in our industry, including those with similar business models, may define or calculate similarly titled measures in different ways, which may limit the usefulness of these measures for direct comparison. In addition, other companies may not publish these or similar metrics. Further, these metrics have certain limitations in that they do not include the impact of certain expenses that are reflected on our consolidated statements of operations. Thus, our non-GAAP financial measures should not be viewed in isolation or as a replacement for the most directly comparable measures prepared in accordance with GAAP.

Non-GAAP Financial Measures
We encourage investors and others to review our business, financial condition, and results of operations in their entirety, not to rely on any single financial measure, and to view our non-GAAP financial measures in conjunction with their respective most directly comparable financial measures calculated in accordance with GAAP, as well as our consolidated financial statements and accompanying notes included elsewhere in this prospectus.

Non-GAAP Financial Measures
The adjusted figures leave out real expenses, and other companies calculate similar measures differently or not at all, so they should be read together with the standard accounting figures and full statements.

Adjusted Operating Income (Loss) and Adjusted Operating Margin
We define Adjusted Operating Income (Loss) as operating loss excluding (i) stock-based compensation expense, (ii) non-cash charitable contributions, and (iii) the Bartz settlement. We define Adjusted Operating Margin as Adjusted Operating Income (Loss) divided by revenue.

Adjusted Operating Income (Loss) and Adjusted Operating Margin
Adjusted Operating Income leaves out pay given in stock, non-cash charitable gifts, and the cost of settling the Bartz lawsuit; Adjusted Operating Margin is that figure divided by revenue.

Since inception, we have financed our operations, corporate investments, and capital expenditures primarily through proceeds from the issuance of convertible promissory notes, redeemable convertible preferred stock, cash generated from sales, and SAFEs. To date, we have financed our compute and infrastructure primarily under arrangements with our CSPs, as well as through proceeds from the financing activities described above and cash generated from operations. As of June 30, 2026, we had cash and cash equivalents of $112.4 billion, $19.3 billion of short-term investments, and $3.2 billion available under the Credit Facility, as described below. Cash and cash equivalents consist of cash held in checking and interest-bearing accounts, money market funds, and other highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or less from the date of purchase.

Anthropic has been funded by investors and sales, with cloud providers supplying compute, and on June 30, 2026 held $112.4B in cash, $19.3B in short-term investments and $3.2B of unused credit.

Liquidity and Capital Resources
We have generated losses from our operations, as reflected in our accumulated deficit of $132.9 billion, which includes $113.2 billion related to changes in the fair value of our convertible notes driven by increases in our enterprise valuation and derivative liabilities since 2023, including $72.4 billion during the six months ended June 30, 2026. Additionally, we have generated negative cash flows from operating and investing activities in 2023, 2024, and 2025, driven by ongoing expenditures to support business growth including investments to secure access to more compute and infrastructure capacity. We continue to invest in our own data center infrastructure and enter into compute and infrastructure capacity arrangements to support anticipated demand for our intelligence service. Given the long lead times between contracting for, purchasing, or leasing compute and that compute becoming available to serve workloads, we secure these arrangements well in advance of anticipated demand.

Liquidity and Capital Resources
To secure certain data center development projects, which require significant capital commitments in advance of deployment, we have in some cases relied, and expect to continue to rely, on arrangements with financing sources or partners who guarantee the lease obligations to support the development of data center capacity that is expected to host such partner’s chips or computing infrastructure. Our ability to expand compute and infrastructure capacity through these arrangements in the future may depend on the continued willingness and ability of a limited number of CSPs, partners, and financing sources to enter into and perform under such arrangements. In some cases, we may also make payments in advance of the delivery of the equipment or infrastructure. We anticipate making significant and increased investments for the foreseeable future, including for owned or leased compute and infrastructure in advance of delivery.

We expect our capital expenditures to increase significantly as we expand our build-out, and we expect these investments to result in significant net cash used in operating and investing activities for the foreseeable future. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures about Market Risk
We are exposed to market risks in the ordinary course of our business. Market risk represents the risk of loss that may impact our financial position due to adverse changes in financial market prices and rates. Our market risk exposure is primarily the result of fluctuations in interest rates and foreign currency exchange rates.

Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures about Market Risk
Anthropic's main financial market risks are changes in interest rates and currency exchange rates.

Interest Rate Risk
As of June 30, 2026, we had $112.4 billion of cash and cash equivalents and $19.3 billion of short-term investments in a variety of securities, including money market funds, U.S. Treasury and agency securities, corporate debt securities, and commercial paper. In addition, we had $2.5 billion of restricted cash primarily due to amounts held as collateral for our lease and other obligations. Our cash, cash equivalents, and shortterm investments are held for working capital purposes, and we do not enter into investments for trading or speculative purposes. Due to the relatively short-term nature of our investment portfolio, a hypothetical 100 basis point increase or decrease in interest rates would not have had a material effect on the fair value of our investment portfolio as of June 30, 2026.

Interest Rate Risk
As of June 30, 2026, Anthropic held $112.4B in cash, $19.3B in short term investments and $2.5B in restricted collateral cash. A one percentage point rate change would not have materially changed their value.

Foreign Currency Exchange Risk
We transact business globally in multiple currencies, with the vast majority of our revenue denominated in U.S. dollars and, to a lesser extent, other currencies such as euros and British pounds. Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs
We elected to account for our convertible notes at fair value pursuant to Accounting Standards Codification (“ASC”) Topic 825, Financial Instruments. The convertible notes are recognized at their estimated fair value on our consolidated balance sheet, and changes in fair value are recorded in change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in our consolidated statement of operations. We elected the fair value option to eliminate the accounting complexity that would otherwise result from separately accounting for the liability and equity components of the convertible notes under the traditional bifurcation model.

Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs
Anthropic chose to carry its convertible notes, which are loans that can turn into shares, at their current estimated market value. Any change in that value hits its reported profit or loss, which avoids splitting each note into a debt piece and a stock piece.

Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs
In connection with the 2023 and 2024 note purchase agreements with both Amazon and Google, we recognized derivative liabilities representing obligations to issue future convertible notes pursuant to the terms of those agreements. The derivative liabilities were measured at estimated fair value, with changes in fair value recorded in change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in the consolidated statement of operations.

Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs
Under its 2023 and 2024 note agreements with Amazon and Google, Anthropic also records its promises to issue more convertible notes later as liabilities, valued at current estimated worth, with value changes flowing into reported profit or loss.

Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs
The estimated fair value of the convertible promissory notes is determined using a hybrid approach comprising a CCA and a CSE method. The analysis estimates the fair value of the convertible promissory notes using a scenario-based analysis that considers the probability-weighted present value of the instruments across the range of possible outcomes available to the note holders, including conversion into redeemable convertible preferred stock, Class N common stock, cash repayment at maturity, and cash settlement at a premium upon a change of control. The scenarios included consider the probability-weighted value of the instruments in the CCA and CSE framework.

Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs
To value the notes, Anthropic combines two valuation methods, called CCA and CSE, that weigh how likely each outcome is: conversion into preferred stock or Class N common stock, repayment in cash at maturity, or a premium cash payout if Anthropic is acquired.

Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs
The application of this methodology involves the use of complex and subjective estimates, judgments, and assumptions, including the probability and timing of each settlement scenario such as a qualified equity financing, initial public offering, direct listing, or change of control; the estimated fair value of our equity securities into which the notes may convert; the applicable conversion prices, which vary by note series and are contingent on factors such as elapsed time since issuance and contractual caps and percentage discounts; and the ownership thresholds and rollover provisions that determine the extent to which principal balances convert into equity versus being reissued as rollover notes.

Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs
In particular, the ownership cap and rollover mechanism— whereby conversion is capped at specified ownership thresholds and any unconverted principal balance is reissued as a non-interest bearing rollover note that remains subject to fair value measurement—requires significant judgment in estimating what proportion of each note financing will convert versus roll over, because this determination depends on the size and structure of future equity financings that are inherently uncertain. Changes in any or all of these estimates and assumptions, or the relationships between those assumptions, impact our valuations as of each measurement date and may have a material impact on the amounts recognized in our consolidated statement of operations.

Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs
These valuations rest on uncertain guesses about the timing and odds of a funding round, IPO, or sale, Anthropic's share value, and how much debt converts versus rolls into new interest-free notes, so reported results can swing materially when assumptions change.
