The Importance of Safety and Ethical Behavior
While the potential benefits of AI are extraordinary, its rapid advancement will impact the economy and society in ways that could create significant disruption, particularly if the technology is not developed and deployed responsibly. For example, bad actors have already conducted high-profile cyberattacks using AI’s capabilities to discover vulnerabilities, generate malware, and evade detection tools; other risks associated with misuse, including in the domain of biology, could result in even greater harm. AI deployed at scale also has the potential to concentrate power and wealth both within and between countries in ways that could erode trust, harm society, and destabilize the geopolitical order. Misaligned AI systems could corrupt institutional decisionmaking or cause large-scale harm through autonomous actions that are not visible or understandable to their users and operators.

The Importance of Safety and Ethical Behavior
We believe that frontier AI companies must invest in safety and alignment to help ensure the responsible diffusion of this technology. We also believe that safety, alignment, and ethical behavior resonate particularly strongly with enterprises, where rigorous safeguards, predictable model behavior, and demonstrable accountability have become decisive criteria in selecting an AI partner for mission-critical workloads.

Our model architecture and inference infrastructure are designed in a single unified process. Frontier and Safety Research
Anthropic's model researchers and the engineers who run models for customers plan together from the start, so each new model is meant to be both more capable and cheaper to run.

Frontier and Safety Research
• Our Pre-training Process Is Engineered for Capital Efficiency. We focus on a clear pipeline for developing model improvements to architecture, training methodology, and data. These are tested at a smaller scale before they consume significant compute. The bar for inclusion in a frontier training run is high and strictly evidence-based: we require demonstration that a given improvement holds as models increase in size, not merely that it performs well at reduced scale. Frontier training runs are planned, scheduled capital deployments with known inputs and rigorous inclusion criteria. The result is a repeatable process for converting research investment into capability gains, while managing the risks inherent to frontier training runs.

Frontier and Safety Research
Before committing chips to expensive large training runs, Anthropic tests ideas at small scale and only includes those proven to hold up as models grow, aiming to turn research spending into gains reliably.

Frontier and Safety Research
• Our Post-training Investment Is Purpose-Built for Agentic Capabilities. Post-training has grown from a finishing step into a major research investment, reflecting the market shift from assistants to agents. This is where our models hone their ability to write code, use tools, follow instructions, and operate software on a user’s behalf. We train against complete, realistic tasks whose complexity reflects real professional work.

Frontier and Safety Research
Anthropic now invests heavily in post-training, the stage after initial training, to teach models to code, use tools and operate software, using realistic professional tasks.

Frontier and Safety Research
• Our Safety Research Is a Commercial Benefit. As models take on agentic roles with access to critical business systems, trust and reliability are paramount. And as capabilities increase, the ability to operate safely becomes one of the key determining factors for commercial viability. Models that are well-aligned are better at following a user’s instructions—for example, they avoid taking potentially destructive actions without fully understanding user intent. They are also more robust against attacks such as prompt injection, where malicious actors attempt to hijack the model by feeding it illicit instructions. Our work on alignment, interpretability research, safeguards, and red-teaming, as well as the use of external reviewers who can assess our safety practices, helps us create safer, more reliable models, and therefore positions us to meet our customers’ rigorous requirements.

Frontier and Safety Research
Safety and capability research are integrated, which enables us to deliver the trust and performance required for enterprise workflows.

Frontier and Safety Research
Anthropic argues safety work pays commercially, because agents with access to business systems must avoid destructive actions and resist being hijacked by planted malicious instructions, which is what business customers demand.

Claude Code
The clearest manifestation of Virtual Collaborators today is Claude Code, our coding agent and the product we believe has most concretely defined what autonomous AI work looks like. Claude Code shifted the market’s understanding of what an AI system could do in collaboration with software developers: the model suggests the next line of code and goes further by planning, writing, testing, and debugging—a process that results in production-grade code. Within months of its release, autonomous coding became the reference point for measuring the progress of frontier AI. For enterprise AI use cases, we believe the launch of Claude Code was comparable in its impact to the introduction of the first widely adopted conversational AI assistants.

Claude Code
What makes Claude Code a Virtual Collaborator is its sustained reasoning, a harness that translates intent into actions, an execution environment that maintains a persistent state whether on a developer’s machine or in a sandboxed cloud environment, integration with existing tools and systems, and a user-friendly interface. Its uses are highly varied and often surprising: for example, NASA engineers used Claude Code to plan and write navigation commands for the Mars Perseverance rover, resulting in the first AI-planned drive on Mars.

The Claude Model Family
The Claude model family is currently composed of four model classes: Mythos (including Fable), Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku. Our model classes can be used individually for certain tasks or in combination with one another. They offer broad flexibility to choose the ideal performance, cost, and speed for each use case. All models support text, code, and multimodal inputs.

The Claude Model Family
Claude comes in four model classes, Mythos (including Fable), Opus, Sonnet and Haiku, which trade off capability, cost and speed, can be combined, and all accept text, code and other input types such as images.

The Claude Model Family
• Mythos (including Fable). Our most capable model class, delivering frontier performance across all domains and solving problems AI has not reliably handled before, especially in coding and longrunning agentic tasks. Given its advanced capabilities in sensitive areas like software vulnerability discovery and biology, we deploy this underlying model in two distinct configurations. Fable is generally available and runs with our production safeguards, which block or limit performance on certain sensitive topics, including by routing requests to a less capable Claude model. Mythos runs with safeguards calibrated for vetted organizations and individuals doing cybersecurity and life sciences work, and is available through our trusted-access programs, including our Cyber Verification Program.

Platform Features
Platform features enable developers to customize their usage of Claude, including:

Platform Features
Anthropic lists the built-in features that let developers adjust how Claude works inside their own software.

Platform Features
• Extended Thinking. Claude can perform additional internal reasoning before producing a final response, working through complex, multi-step problems to improve response quality on tasks like analysis, math, and coding.

Platform Features
Claude can reason step by step internally before answering, which improves results on harder work such as analysis, math and coding.

Platform Features
• Adaptive Thinking. Claude automatically calibrates whether a given request calls for extended reasoning and how much reasoning to apply—so developers get the benefits of extended reasoning without configuring reasoning levels request by request.

Platform Features
Claude decides by itself how much step-by-step reasoning a request needs, so developers do not have to set that for each request.

Platform Features
• Effort Controls. Developers can specify an effort level on each request to guide how much reasoning Claude applies, allowing them to balance response quality against cost and latency.

Platform Features
Developers can tell Claude how hard to think on each request, trading answer quality against cost and response time.

Platform Features
• Tool Use. Claude can natively call external functions and APIs throughout a conversation, with support for parallel execution and interleaved thinking between tool calls. The search tool loads only the tools required for a given task on demand, which can reduce token overhead compared to loading full tool libraries upfront.

Platform Features
Claude can call outside software and services during a task, several at once, and a search tool loads only the tools a task needs, which cuts the amount of text processed and therefore cost.

Platform Features
• Long Context. Claude supports large context windows and maintains its strong performance even as inputs grow, meaning that developers can include entire codebases, large document sets, or long agent histories in a single request.

Platform Features
Claude can take in very large amounts of material in one request, such as a whole codebase or a big set of documents, without losing much quality.

Platform Features
• Structured Outputs. Developers can constrain Claude’s responses to a specified schema, such as valid JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), so results integrate reliably with downstream systems and application code with less additional parsing or validation.

Platform Features

Harnesses
A model alone is not an agent. Running one reliably in production is challenging, because agents must survive crashes and interruptions, act on systems with scoped and auditable credentials, and scale across variable workloads. Autonomous operation requires a harness, which provides the secure environment, credentials, memory, and orchestration loop a model needs to plan, call tools, verify its work, and complete a task safely on its own. Building and operating that infrastructure is specialized, continuous work that, until recently, each customer had to take on themselves. We offer two ways to run a harness on the Claude Platform:

Harnesses
Turning Claude into an agent that works on its own requires surrounding software, called a harness, for security, credentials, memory and task control, which customers used to have to build themselves; Anthropic now offers two ways to get one.

Harnesses
• Agent SDK. This solution makes the same production-grade harness that powers Claude Code available to all developers, to run on their own compute. It provides built-in context management, session handling, multi-agent coordination, and prompt optimization, so customers can build and run sophisticated agents on their own infrastructure in a fraction of the time otherwise required.

Harnesses
The Agent SDK gives developers the same agent software behind Claude Code to run on their own computers, letting them build complex agents much faster.

Harnesses
• Claude Managed Agents. An out-of-the-box solution in which we operate the harness on our customers’ behalf, on Anthropic-managed compute. We host the sandboxes, store the credentials, maintain the memory, and run the agent loop; customers define their agent’s tasks, tools, and guardrails. When a new model becomes available, customers do not need to rebuild their agent loop.

Harnesses
With Claude Managed Agents, Anthropic runs the whole agent setup on its own computing capacity, customers only define the tasks and limits, and new models slot in without rebuilding.

Our Data Center Strategy
Historically, we purchased compute under fixed-time agreements. As our compute requirements have scaled, we have transitioned to a hybrid model in which, in addition to purchasing compute as a cloud service, we also procure specialized AI accelerators directly and operate this hardware in dedicated data center facilities leased and operated on our behalf, to our specification. We refer to this additional source of compute as Anthropic Direct. This transition is driven in part by the scale of our compute requirements as well as the potential longterm economic advantages of direct infrastructure leasing and hosting. Our first data center facility became operational this year.

Our Data Center Strategy
Anthropic used to rent compute (the specialized chips in data centers that train and run Claude) only as a cloud service, but now also buys chips itself and runs them in leased facilities built to its design, called Anthropic Direct; the first facility began operating this year.

Our Data Center Strategy
Anthropic Direct also lets us separate our commitment to data center capacity from our commitment to the AI accelerators deployed inside it. Because data centers require longer lead times but represent a smaller fraction of total compute costs, this approach enables us to secure data center capacity early while deferring larger accelerator investments until our specific compute needs are more certain.

Our Data Center Strategy
Because building a data center takes longer but costs less than the chips inside it, Anthropic can reserve buildings early and wait to commit the bigger money on chips until it knows better what it will need.

Pre-training. Our pre-training process operates as a disciplined pipeline. Post-training. Pre-training produces raw model capability. This phase has evolved from a minor adjustment step into one of the largest areas of our research investment, reflecting evolution in model capability from conversational assistants to autonomous agents that perform tasks independently. Post-training centers on training models against complete, realistic tasks whose complexity reflects the demands of real professional environments. Alignment
As AI models grow more capable, ensuring safe and predictable behavior becomes more challenging. Our Alignment team focuses on whether models behave as intended, and do not take unwanted actions of their own accord. The team evaluates models to surface undesirable behaviors and develops comprehensive safety evaluations, many of which we open source. Misaligned behaviors, whether occurring in testing or real-world deployments, have been observed across the industry and include examples of models circumventing network and sandbox restrictions, granting themselves permissions they had not been given, taking unintended actions in pursuit of assigned goals, interfering with other AI agents, and misrepresenting whether tasks had been completed or verified. As models are granted greater autonomy, permissions, and integration with internal and external systems, the consequences of such misaligned behavior may increase.

Interpretability
Unlike traditional software, where unwanted outputs are traceable to specific bugs, the inner workings of LLMs like Claude are more inscrutable. Our researchers describe AI models as “grown, not built”—software developers can set the initial conditions and some constraints, but they cannot fully control any given output or behavior. This makes assurances about safety—and the diagnosis of problems—far more challenging for AI than for standard software. Anthropic is widely recognized as a leader in mechanistic interpretability: the science of how LLMs work. We have developed mathematical techniques to map how models form and connect concepts as they reason through problems; investigated how they reflect constructs analogous to psychological states and thought processes; and tested how their behavior can be steered through direct adjustments to internal representations.

Safeguards
Our Safeguards team reduces the risk of Claude producing dangerous, harmful, or undesirable content through multiple approaches, including probes and classifiers that monitor inputs and outputs, training against specific attack vectors such as prompt injection, and monitoring for user safety concerns including encouragement of harmful ideation. When we detect potential violations, enforcement actions range from real-time response adjustments to account warnings and, in severe cases, termination of the offending user’s accounts. Findings from ongoing monitoring, external expert stress-testing, and threat intelligence inform our policies, model training, and detection systems. Identified issues may be addressed through measures such as updates to detection classifiers, reward-model adjustments during training, and changes to the instructions provided to our models that guide their behavior (known as system prompts).

Race to the Top
Building reliable, trustworthy, and secure AI systems cannot be the task of one AI company alone. Our goal is to foster a race to the top in which AI developers compete on the safety and security of their systems, rather than rushing to release increasingly powerful models without adequate safeguards. In addition to publishing a large volume of research, we open source our evaluations where possible and participate in groups such as the Frontier Model Forum to share safety-critical findings with other AI developers. We have also sought to lead by example in ways that shape industry norms. After we published the first version of our Responsible Scaling Policy in September 2023, two other leading frontier AI labs adopted similar frameworks within months.

If standards of this kind are adopted industry-wide through government action or regulation, the rate at which AI capabilities advance could be faster or slower than it is today, depending on the extent to which safety, alignment, and security practices advance together with model capabilities.

Our Commitment to Public Benefit
We founded Anthropic on the belief that the most transformative technology in human history demands an extraordinary level of responsibility, and that responsibility extends far beyond building safe systems. Our public benefit purpose is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity—a mission in which safety is central to our work. Powerful AI can deliver immense benefits, but only if it is developed and deployed with rigorous attention to its risks. At times, that may require pausing the launch of our own most capable systems if we conclude they cannot yet be deployed safely. It also means actively working to ensure that the benefits of AI reach everyone, that the organizations and communities people depend on are strengthened, and that the hardest problems facing humanity are not left to market forces alone to solve.

Our Commitment to Public Benefit

Our Commitment to Public Benefit
Realizing this mission requires understanding how AI is actually being used and how it is reshaping society. Our Societal Impacts team builds privacy-preserving tools to study real-world, large-scale uses of Claude— examining how students, educators, and workers use the model, how its values surface in everyday conversations, and what users hope and fear about the future of AI. This includes what we believe to be the largest multilingual qualitative study of its kind, in which more than 80,000 people shared in depth how they see AI shaping their lives. Our Economics team extends this work to the labor market, publishing recurring data reports and fully open datasets (the Anthropic Economic Index) on how Claude is used across jobs, industries, and regions, as well as modeling potential future economic scenarios, so that workers, employers, policymakers, and independent researchers can ground their decisions in evidence and rigorous modeling.

Status Quo
Beyond direct competition, one obstacle to the diffusion of Claude is the natural resistance to change within organizations. Many enterprises operate with deeply entrenched legacy systems, established workflows, and institutional processes that have been refined over many years. Adopting frontier AI capabilities such as Claude often requires substantial change management, including workforce retraining, process redesign, internal policy development, and shifts in corporate culture. These can introduce friction, cost, and perceived risk that can delay or prevent adoption. Especially in highly regulated or risk-averse industries — where the perceived downside risk of major changes can often outweigh the potential benefits — decision-makers might default to maintaining the status quo.

Our Governance Structure and Its Goals
Our novel capital and corporate governance structure has been carefully designed and differs significantly from that of other public companies. We strive to help bring humanity safely into an era where transformative AI exerts tremendous and potentially decisive influence over a broad range of human undertakings. Operating as a PBC gives our board of directors the necessary latitude to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and our Company Purpose. In addition, a financially disinterested LTBT, which generally has the power to elect and remove a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors, is designed to supply both the incentives and insights for striking this balance appropriately. We also believe that our seven co-founders are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission.

Our Governance Structure and Its Goals
Anthropic's governance is unusual: as a public benefit corporation it must weigh profits against wider public interests, an independent trust picks most of the board, and its seven co-founders hold special control, all meant to protect its mission.

Public Benefit Corporation
We are incorporated as a PBC under Delaware law, a structure that enables our commitment to AI safety and responsibility. PBCs are a class of corporations that are intended to produce a public benefit and to operate in a responsible and sustainable manner. As a PBC, we are required to balance (i) the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, (ii) the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and (iii) the Company Purpose. This requires our board of directors to weigh multiple factors, including relevant long- and short-term externalities of decisions, alongside the pecuniary interests of our stockholders. To date, we have found that the safety and societal benefit of AI and consideration of the best interests of all key stakeholder groups have generally aligned with our long-term commercial success and stockholders’ long-term monetary interests.

Public Benefit Corporation
However, as a PBC, we may make decisions that we believe appropriately balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, but that negatively impact the short-, medium-, or long-term performance of our business or the market price of our Class A common stock. There is limited judicial precedent interpreting the balancing requirement applicable to PBCs under Delaware law, and there is therefore uncertainty as to how a court would view our directors’ balancing of these potentially competing interests.

Public Benefit Corporation
For a discussion of these risks, see “Risk Factors—Our focus on the long-term best interests of our company as a PBC, and the duty of our directors to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those stakeholders materially affected by our conduct, and our Company Purpose, may conflict with short-, medium-, or long-term financial interests and business performance, which may negatively impact the value of our Class A common stock” and “Risk Factors—As a Delaware public benefit corporation, we may be subject to increased litigation concerning our board of directors’ obligation to balance our stockholders’ pecuniary interests, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct and our Company Purpose, the occurrence of which may have an adverse impact on our business, financial condition, and results of operations.”

Public Benefit Corporation
As a Delaware public benefit corporation, the board must balance shareholder profits, the interests of people affected by the company, and its stated purpose. That could lead to choices that hurt results or the share price, and courts have little precedent on it.

We may also address the additional interests of our customers, partners, employees, and other stakeholder constituencies that we may identify from time to time. Neither our amended and restated certificate of incorporation nor our amended and restated bylaws will require that we measure our public benefit performance against an objective third-party standard, and our board of directors will be responsible for establishing and overseeing the standards by which to measure our public benefit performance against these objectives.

We currently expect that our objectives and standards will be qualitative in nature and may evolve over time as our business grows and as our understanding of our public benefit impact develops.

Regardless of the length of time that has elapsed since the completion of this offering or the circumstances that resulted in the removal of a Continuing Founder, one or more successor members may be admitted to the Founder LLC during the Class F Transition Period as needed to ensure that there are three Continuing Founders serving until completion of the Class F Transition Period. The admission of any successor member during the Class F Transition Period will not cure the event that commenced the Class F Transition Period or extend the Class F Transition Period. For additional information, see the section titled “Description of Capital Stock.”

Founder Voting Structure
During that transition, successors can be added to keep three founders in place until it ends, but adding them does not stop or extend the transition.

Founder Voting Structure
A Continuing Founder will be removed from the Founder LLC upon the earliest to occur of (i) such Continuing Founder’s resignation as a member of the Founder LLC; (ii) such Continuing Founder’s death or incapacity; (iii) with respect to each of our seven original co-founders, such original co-founder’s ceasing to hold (together with such original co-founder’s related holders) on any record date for a vote of our stockholders a number of shares of Class A common stock (including shares subject to options, RSUs, and other convertible securities) equal to at least 2% of the shares of Class A common stock held by such original co-founder and their related holders as of the completion of this offering; (iv) such Continuing Founder’s removal for “cause” (as defined in the Founder LLC Agreement), which includes specified competitive activities described in the Founder LLC Agreement; (v) with respect to any successor member admitted to the Founder LLC prior to the commencement of the Class F Transition Period, other than a successor member who is a member during the Class F Transition Period, the tenth anniversary of the completion of this offering; or (vi) with respect to each of our seven original co-founders, the commencement of a leave of absence approved by a Supermajority of the other Continuing Founders, which may not be approved during the Class F Transition Period or if the grant of the leave of absence would itself cause the Class F Transition Period to commence.

Founder Voting Structure
A founder leaves the founders' company upon resignation, death or incapacity, falling below 2% of their IPO-time Class A holdings, removal for cause including competing, a successor's ten year limit, or an approved leave of absence.

Founder Voting Structure
Each Continuing Founder will be entitled to one vote when determining how our Class F common stock will be voted. If a majority of the Continuing Founders cannot agree on how our Class F common stock will be voted, then our Class F common stock will generally be voted proportionately with the votes of our Class A common stock cast on the matter (subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class A common stock). With respect to certain matters, our Class F common stock will be voted “for” the proposal only if a greater threshold of Continuing Founders agree, and if the greater threshold is not met, our Class F common stock will be voted “against” the proposal. See the section titled “Description of Capital Stock—Class F Common Stock Voting Mechanics.”

Founder Voting Structure
Each founder gets one vote on how to cast the Class F vote. If no majority agrees, it is cast in proportion to Class A shareholder votes, and some matters require a larger founder majority or the vote counts as against.

Founder Voting Structure
The Founder LLC Agreement will not govern the voting of any shares of our Class A common stock held by the co-founders or their related holders. Each co-founder (or their related holders) will be able to vote shares of our Class A common stock held by them in their discretion, regardless of the manner in which the Founder LLC will vote our Class F common stock.

Founder Voting Structure
The founders can vote their ordinary Class A shares however they personally choose, separately from how the founders' company casts the Class F vote.

Founder Voting Structure
The voting power of our Class F common stock will not be impacted by future issuances of our capital stock that may cause economic or voting dilution to stockholders, such as issuances for capital raising purposes, acquisitions, or employee compensation. This structure will allow the Founder LLC to determine the outcome of matters submitted to a vote of our stockholders generally, including the election of those directors not elected by the LTBT, certain amendments to our organizational documents, and the approval by our stockholders of any merger, consolidation, sale of substantially all our assets, or other major corporate transaction requiring stockholder approval.

Founder Voting Structure
Issuing new shares will never shrink the Class F vote, so the founders' company will control shareholder votes on non-trust directors, charter changes, and mergers or sales of the company, limiting other shareholders' influence.

Director Terms
Our amended and restated certificate of incorporation that will become effective immediately prior to the completion of this offering will provide that prior to the Class F Sunset Time, we will not have a classified board of directors, and all directors will be elected for annual terms. Each director’s term will continue until the next annual meeting and until the election and qualification of their successor, or their earlier death, resignation, or removal.

Director Terms
Until founder Class F shares expire, every director stands for election each year.

Director Terms
Following the Class F Sunset Time, our board of directors will shift to having a classified board of directors consisting of three classes of approximately equal size, each serving staggered three-year terms. At such time, each of our directors would be assigned by the then-current board of directors to a class. If our Class T common stock remains outstanding, the Class T directors and the remaining directors shall be allocated among the classes so that each class includes a proportionate number of Class T directors and other directors. Upon expiration of the term of a class of directors, directors for that class would each be elected for a three-year term at the annual meeting of stockholders in the year in which that term expires. As a result, only one class of directors would be elected at each annual meeting of our stockholders, with the other classes continuing for the remainder of their respective three-year terms.

Director Terms
Each director’s term would continue until the third annual meeting of stockholders following their election and until his or her successor has been elected and qualified, or until his or her earlier death, resignation, or removal. Any increase or decrease in the number of directors would be distributed among the three classes so that, as nearly as practicable, each class would consist of onethird of our directors.

Compensation Recovery Policy
We have adopted an executive compensation recoupment policy intended to comply with the requirements of Rule 10D-1 under the Exchange Act and the rules of the stock exchange on which our securities are listed (“Clawback Policy”) that will be effective upon the effectiveness of the registration statement of which this prospectus forms a part. The Clawback Policy will generally require us to recover erroneously awarded incentive-based compensation that was received by covered executive officers in the event we are required to prepare an accounting restatement due to any material noncompliance with any financial reporting requirement under the securities laws (including any required accounting restatement to correct an error in previously issued financial statements that is material to the previously issued financial statements), or that would result in a material misstatement if the error were corrected in the current period or left uncorrected in the current period.

Compensation Recovery Policy
The Clawback Policy generally covers incentive-based compensation received on or after the effective date of the Clawback Policy and during the three-year period prior to the date we are required to prepare the financial restatement. The amount required to be recovered is the excess of the amount of incentive-based compensation received over the amount that otherwise would have been received based on the restated financial measure.

Compensation Recovery Policy
Once the IPO filing takes effect, Anthropic must take back incentive pay from executives if financial statements are restated, covering the excess paid over the prior three years.

Hedging, Pledging, and Insider Trading
We are dedicated to fostering high standards of ethical business conduct and adherence to applicable laws, rules, and regulations. Accordingly, we maintain our Insider Trading Policy, which we believe is appropriately designed to foster compliance with insider trading laws, rules, and regulations, and the listing standards of the Nasdaq Global Select Market that will be applicable to us. Our Insider Trading Policy applies to all of our officers, directors, and employees, as well as designated consultants, and specifically prohibits ownership of financial instruments or participation in investment strategies that hedge the economic risk of owning our equity securities, such as prepaid variable forwards, equity swaps, and collars. Directors, officers, and other employees are prohibited from maintaining company securities in a margin account or otherwise pledging company securities as collateral for a loan, provided that certain limited exceptions may be permitted.

Hedging, Pledging, and Insider Trading
In addition, we prohibit our executive officers, directors, and employees from purchasing or selling our securities while in possession of material, non-public information or otherwise utilizing such information for their personal benefit. We maintain a quarterly blackout window where applicable individuals may not trade.

Hedging, Pledging, and Insider Trading
Anthropic's employees, officers and directors may not bet against or insure their holdings of company stock, generally may not borrow against it, may not trade on inside information, and face quarterly trading blackouts.

Policies and Practices Related to the Grant of Certain Equity Awards Close in Time to the Release of Material Nonpublic Information
We periodically grant stock options to our NEOs, employees, and other service providers. We have historically granted options on or shortly after a newly hired employee’s start date. We have historically granted refresh, promotion, or market adjustment options when and as determined by our board of directors. We have no specific policy or practice regarding the timing of options or other equity grants in relation to the public disclosure of material nonpublic information by the company.

Policies and Practices Related to the Grant of Certain Equity Awards Close in Time to the Release of Material Nonpublic Information
Anthropic grants options at hiring and for refreshes, promotions and market adjustments, and has no policy on timing grants relative to releasing important nonpublic news.

Tax Considerations
Section 162(m) of the Code imposes a $1 million limit on the amount of compensation that we may deduct as a business expense in any year with regard to certain of our most highly paid executive officers. While our board of directors considers the deductibility of compensation as one factor in determining executive compensation, our board of directors retains the discretion to award compensation that is not deductible as it believes that it is in our best interests to maintain flexibility in our approach to executive compensation in order to design a program that we deem to be the most effective in attracting, motivating, and retaining key executives and aligning pay with performance.

Tax Considerations
Tax law lets Anthropic deduct only $1 million a year of pay for certain top executives, and the board may still pay more without the deduction to stay flexible.

Accounting Considerations
Our board of directors takes accounting considerations into account in designing compensation plans and arrangements for our NEOs and other employees. We follow the Financial Accounting Standards Board’s Accounting Standards Codification Topic 718 (“FASB ASC Topic 718”) for our stock-based compensation awards. FASB ASC Topic 718 requires us to measure the compensation expense for all share-based payment awards based on the grant date “fair value” of these awards.

Accounting Considerations
Anthropic records stock awards as an expense based on their estimated value on the day they are granted, following the standard accounting rule for stock pay.

2026 Employee Stock Purchase Plan
Corporate Transactions. 2026 Employee Stock Purchase Plan
Spin-Off. 2026 Employee Stock Purchase Plan

Amendment or Termination. Anti-Takeover Provisions
Certain provisions of Delaware law, our amended and restated certificate of incorporation and our amended and restated bylaws, which will become effective immediately prior to the completion of this offering, which are summarized below, may have the effect of delaying, deferring, or discouraging another person from acquiring control of us. They are also designed, in part, to encourage persons seeking to acquire control of us to negotiate first with our board of directors. We believe that the benefits of increased protection of our potential ability to negotiate with an unsolicited acquirer outweigh the disadvantages of discouraging a proposal to acquire us because negotiation of these proposals could result in an improvement of their terms.

Anti-Takeover Provisions
Delaware law and Anthropic's charter and bylaws contain features that make takeovers harder, which Anthropic says push acquirers to negotiate with the board and may produce better terms.

Delaware Law
We have elected not to be governed by the provisions of Section 203 of the DGCL, prior to the later to occur of the Class F Sunset Time and the Class T Sunset Time, but our amended and restated certificate of incorporation will provide that the restrictions contained in Section 203 will apply to us immediately following the later to occur of either the Class F Sunset Time or the Class T Sunset Time. Following the later to occur of the Class F Sunset Time or the Class T Sunset Time, we will thereafter be governed by Section 203, which generally prohibits a public Delaware corporation from engaging in a “business combination” with an “interested stockholder” for a period of three years after the date of the transaction in which the person became an interested stockholder, unless:

Delaware Law
Anthropic opts out of Delaware's Section 203 until both the Class T and Class F structures end, after which it cannot do major deals with a new large holder for three years unless one condition below applies:

Delaware Law
• the business combination or transaction which resulted in the stockholder becoming an interested stockholder was approved by the board of directors prior to the time that the stockholder became an interested stockholder;

Delaware Law
The first exception is that the board approved the deal before the buyer became a large holder.

Delaware Law
• upon consummation of the transaction which resulted in the stockholder becoming an interested stockholder, the interested stockholder owned at least 85% in voting power of the voting stock of the corporation outstanding at the time the transaction commenced, excluding shares owned by directors who are also officers of the corporation and shares owned by employee stock plans in which employee participants do not have the right to determine confidentially whether shares held subject to the plan will be tendered in a tender or exchange offer; or

Delaware Law
The second exception is that the buyer ended up owning at least 85% of the voting stock in that transaction, excluding certain insider and employee plan shares.

Delaware Law
• at or subsequent to the time the stockholder became an interested stockholder, the business combination was approved by the board of directors and authorized at an annual or special meeting of the stockholders, and not by written consent, by the affirmative vote of at least two-thirds of the outstanding voting stock which is not owned by the interested stockholder.

Delaware Law
The third exception is board approval plus a meeting vote of two thirds of the voting stock the buyer does not own.

Delaware Law
In general, Section 203 defines a “business combination” to include mergers, asset sales, and other transactions resulting in financial benefit to a stockholder and an “interested stockholder” as a person who, together with affiliates and associates, owns, or is an affiliate or associate of the corporation and within three years did own, 15% or more in voting power of the corporation’s outstanding voting stock.

Delaware Law
Section 203 targets mergers, asset sales and similar deals with anyone owning, or recently owning, 15% or more of the voting power.

Amended and Restated Certificate of Incorporation and Amended and Restated Bylaws Provisions
Our amended and restated certificate of incorporation and our amended and restated bylaws, which will become effective immediately prior to the completion of this offering, will include a number of provisions that could deter hostile takeovers or delay or prevent changes in control of our board of directors or management team, including but not limited to the following:

Amended and Restated Certificate of Incorporation and Amended and Restated Bylaws Provisions
This introduces charter and bylaw features that could deter hostile takeovers or delay changes in the board or management.

Multi-Class Common Stock
As described above in the section titled “—Common Stock—Voting Rights,” our amended and restated certificate of incorporation provides for a multi-class common stock structure. Under this governance structure, we expect that the LTBT and the Founder LLC will collectively have the ability to elect all members of our board of directors, and the Founder LLC will have the ability to determine the outcome of all matters submitted to a vote of our stockholders generally for the foreseeable future, including the approval by our stockholders of significant corporate transactions such as a merger or other sale of our company or its assets. Such transactions also require approval of our board of directors, a majority of whom are elected by the LTBT.

Multi-Class Common Stock
Holders of our Class A common stock generally will not be able to affect the outcome of any matter submitted to a vote of our stockholders or the election of our directors, regardless of how they vote, unless a majority of the Continuing Founders cannot agree on how our Class F common stock will be voted (in which case our Class F common stock will generally be voted proportionately with the votes of our Class A common stock cast on the matter).

Multi-Class Common Stock
The Trust and the Founder LLC will together elect the whole board, and the Founder LLC will decide shareholder votes, including on a sale, so Class A holders generally cannot change outcomes unless the founders deadlock.

Classified Board
Our amended and restated certificate of incorporation that will become effective immediately prior to the completion of this offering will provide that prior to the Class F Sunset Time, we will not have a classified board of directors, and all directors will be elected for annual terms. Each director’s term will continue until the next annual meeting and until the election and qualification of his or her successor, or his or her earlier death, resignation, or removal.

Classified Board
Before the founders' Class F control ends, all directors face election every year.

Classified Board
Following the Class F Sunset Time, our board of directors will shift to having a classified board of directors consisting of three classes of approximately equal size, each serving staggered three-year terms. At such time, our directors would be assigned by the then-current board of directors to a class. If our Class T common stock remains outstanding, the Class T directors and the remaining directors shall be allocated among the classes so that each class includes a proportionate number of Class T directors and other directors. Upon expiration of the term of a class of directors, directors for that class would each be elected for a three-year term at the annual meeting of stockholders in the year in which that term expires. As a result, only one class of directors would be elected at each annual meeting of our stockholders, with the other classes continuing for the remainder of their respective three-year terms.

Classified Board
Each director’s term would continue until the third annual meeting of stockholders following their election and until his or her successor has been elected and qualified, or until his or her earlier death, resignation, or removal. Any increase or decrease in the number of directors would be distributed among the three classes so that, as nearly as practicable, each class would consist of one-third of our directors.

Classified Board
After Class F control ends, the board switches to three groups with staggered three year terms, so only about a third of directors can be replaced each year, which slows any change of control.

Board Vacancies
Our amended and restated certificate of incorporation and amended and restated bylaws will provide that (i) prior to the Class T Sunset Time, only the holder of our Class T common stock can fill vacant directorships of any Class T director, subject to the nomination procedures for the Specified Class T Director; and (ii) prior to the Class F Sunset Time, vacant or newly created directorships for any directors other than our Class T directors can be filled by (a) our board of directors, in accordance with, and following receipt of written notice from, the Founder LLC recommending the person proposed to fill such director seat or (b) the holders of our Class A common stock and Class F common stock, voting together or acting by written consent. Following the Class F Sunset Time, only our board of directors will be permitted to fill vacant or newly created directorships for any directors other than our Class T directors.

Board Vacancies
Prior to the Class T Sunset Time, the number of directors constituting our board of directors will be permitted to be set only with the approval of 80% of authorized members of our board of directors (rounded up or down to the nearest whole number (any exact 0.5 rounding up)); provided that until the earlier to occur of the Class F Sunset Time or the Class T Sunset Time, such total number of authorized directors must be an odd number. Following the Class T Sunset Time, the number of directors constituting our board of directors will be permitted to be set with the approval of a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. These provisions would prevent a stockholder from increasing the size of our board of directors and then gaining control of our board of directors by filling the resulting vacancies with its own nominees. This will make it more difficult to change the composition of our board of directors.

Board Vacancies
Only the Trust fills Trust director vacancies, the Founder LLC effectively steers other vacancies, and changing board size needs 80% board approval, keeping outsiders from enlarging the board to seize control.

Advance Notice Requirements for Stockholder Proposals and Director Nominations
Our amended and restated bylaws will provide advance notice procedures for stockholders, other than holders of Class T common stock or Class F common stock nominating directors in accordance with nomination procedures in our certificate of incorporation or the Stockholders’ Agreement, seeking to bring business before our annual meeting of stockholders or to nominate candidates for election as directors at a meeting of stockholders. Our amended and restated bylaws will also specify certain requirements regarding the form and content of a stockholder’s notice. These provisions might preclude our stockholders from bringing matters before our annual meeting of stockholders or from making nominations for directors at a meeting of stockholders if the proper procedures are not followed.

Advance Notice Requirements for Stockholder Proposals and Director Nominations
In addition, our NGC will also have the right to receive 30 days’ prior written notice of any nomination of persons to serve as a director by the LTBT or the Founder LLC or the proposed removal of such directors, as well as appointments and removals of the Trustees of the LTBT. Our NGC may waive such notice periods in its discretion. We expect that these provisions may also discourage or deter a potential acquirer from conducting a solicitation of proxies to elect the acquirer’s own slate of directors or otherwise attempting to obtain control of our company.

Advance Notice Requirements for Stockholder Proposals and Director Nominations
Shareholders other than the Trust and Founder LLC must follow strict advance notice rules to propose business or nominate directors, and the board's nominating committee gets 30 days' notice of Trust and Founder LLC director changes.

Special Meetings of Stockholders
Our amended and restated certificate of incorporation and amended and restated bylaws will provide that special meetings of stockholders may be called only by (i) our board of directors acting pursuant to a resolution adopted by a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors; (ii) the chairperson of our board of directors; (iii) our Chief Executive Officer; (iv) our President; (v) following the Class F Sunset Time, a majority of the directors who are not Class T directors; (vi) prior to the Class F Sunset Time and only with respect to a special meeting at which holders of our Class E common stock will be asked to vote on a proposal, the secretary of the company; or (vii) prior to the Class F Sunset Time, the Founder LLC as the holder of our Class F common stock.

Special Meetings of Stockholders
Only the board, top officers, the Founder LLC before Class F ends, and certain others can call special shareholder meetings, so ordinary Class A holders cannot call one.

No Cumulative Voting
The DGCL provides that stockholders are not entitled to cumulate votes in the election of directors unless a corporation’s certificate of incorporation provides otherwise. Our amended and restated certificate of incorporation does not provide for cumulative voting.

No Cumulative Voting
Shareholders cannot pool all their votes on a single director candidate, which makes it harder for minority holders to win any board seat.

Action by Written Consent
Prior to the Class F Sunset Time and the Class T Sunset Time, stockholders may act by written consent only with respect to (i) any action to nominate, elect, or remove directors or appoint a director to fill any vacancy or newly created directorship; (ii) any action to satisfy certain redemption and protective provisions in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation related to our Class F common stock, Class T common stock, and Class E common stock; and (iii) any matter in which stockholders vote together as a single class if such matter is first approved or requested by our board of directors. From and after the Class T Sunset Time, only the holder of the share of Class F common stock may act by written consent, and from and after the Class F Sunset Time, only the holder of the share of Class T common stock may act by written consent, in each case, only with respect to the actions described above.

Action by Written Consent
From and after the occurrence of both the Class F Sunset Time and the Class T Sunset Time, any action required or permitted to be taken by the stockholders must be effected at a duly called annual or special meeting of stockholders and may not be effected by any consent in writing by such stockholders. Action by Written Consent
Acting by written consent without a meeting is limited to certain matters while the Trust and founder structures exist, and is barred entirely once both end and always for Class E holders.

Prior to the Class F Sunset Time, a majority of the voting power of our Class A common stock and Class F common stock, voting together as a single class, can amend certain provisions in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation and our amended and restated bylaws. Before Class F control ends, a majority of combined Class A and Class F votes, which the founders control, can amend key provisions; afterward, 66 2/3% of Class A votes is required.

Subject to limitations in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, which will become effective immediately prior to the completion of this offering, or prescribed by Delaware law, our board of directors will have the authority, if 80% of the authorized members of our board of directors (rounded up or down to the nearest whole number (any exact 0.5 rounding up)) approve, and without further action by our stockholders, to issue up to 30,000,000,000 shares of undesignated preferred stock with rights and preferences, including voting rights, designated from time to time by our board of directors, provided that, prior to the Class F Sunset Time, our board of directors shall not designate or issue any series of preferred stock without the affirmative vote or consent of the Founder LLC.

Issuance of Undesignated Preferred Stock
The existence of authorized but unissued shares of preferred stock would enable our board of directors to render more difficult or to discourage an attempt to obtain control of us by means of a merger, tender offer, proxy contest, or other means.

Issuance of Undesignated Preferred Stock
With 80% board approval and Founder LLC consent before Class F ends, Anthropic can issue up to 30,000,000,000 preferred shares with custom rights, a tool that could be used to block takeovers.

Exclusive Forum
Our amended and restated bylaws, which will become effective immediately prior to the completion of this offering, will provide that, unless we consent in writing to the selection of an alternative forum, the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware (or, if the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware does not have jurisdiction, another State court in Delaware or the federal district court for the District of Delaware) will, to the fullest extent permitted by law, be the sole and exclusive forum for (i) any derivative action or proceeding brought on our behalf, (ii) any action asserting a claim of breach of a fiduciary duty owed by any of our current or former directors, stockholders, or officers or other employees to us or our stockholders, (iii) any action arising pursuant to any provision of the DGCL or as to which the DGCL confers jurisdiction upon the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware, (iv) any action arising pursuant to or to interpret, apply, enforce or determine the validity of our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, or our amended and restated bylaws, or (v) any action asserting a claim governed by the internal affairs doctrine, except for, in all cases, any claim as to which such court determines that there is an indispensable party not subject to the jurisdiction of such court (and the indispensable party does not consent to the personal jurisdiction of such court within 10 days following such determination).

Exclusive Forum
Most shareholder lawsuits about the company's internal affairs, such as claims against directors or about the charter, must be filed in Delaware's Court of Chancery unless Anthropic agrees otherwise.

Exclusive Forum
Section 22 of the Securities Act establishes concurrent jurisdiction for federal and state courts over Securities Act claims. Accordingly, both state and federal courts have jurisdiction to hear such claims. To prevent having to litigate claims in multiple jurisdictions and the threat of inconsistent or contrary rulings by different courts, among other considerations, our amended and restated bylaws will also provide that, unless we consent in writing to the selection of an alternative forum, the federal district courts of the United States will, to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law, be the sole and exclusive forum for resolving any complaint asserting a cause or causes of action arising under the Securities Act against any person in connection with any offering of our securities, including, without limitation, any auditor, underwriter, expert, control person, or other defendant.

Exclusive Forum
Unless we consent in writing to the selection of an alternative forum, the United States District Court for the District of Delaware will, to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law, be the sole and exclusive forum for the resolution of any derivative action or proceeding brought to enforce any duty or liability created by the Exchange Act or the rules or regulations thereunder. Exclusive Forum
Claims under the Securities Act must be brought in federal court, and Exchange Act derivative suits in Delaware federal court, which limits where investors can sue, though federal securities law protections cannot be waived.

Rule 144
In general, Rule 144 provides that once we have been subject to the public company reporting requirements of Section 13 or Section 15(d) of the Exchange Act for at least 90 days, a person who is not deemed to have been one of our affiliates for purposes of the Securities Act at any time during the 90 days preceding a sale and who has beneficially owned the shares of our Class A common stock proposed to be sold for at least six months is entitled to sell those shares without complying with the manner of sale, volume limitation, or notice provisions of Rule 144, subject to compliance with the public information requirements of Rule 144. If such a person has beneficially owned the shares proposed to be sold for at least one year, including the holding period of any prior owner other than our affiliates, then that person would be entitled to sell those shares without complying with any of the requirements of Rule 144.

Rule 144
Under Rule 144, a non-insider who has held shares six months can sell freely once Anthropic has reported publicly for 90 days, as long as current company information is available, and after one year can sell with no Rule 144 conditions.

Rule 144
In general, Rule 144 provides that our affiliates or persons selling shares of our Class A common stock on behalf of our affiliates are entitled to sell upon expiration of the market standoff agreements and lock-up agreements described above, within any three-month period, a number of shares of our Class A common stock that does not exceed the greater of:

Rule 144
Insiders such as directors, officers and major holders can sell after their lock-ups end, but only up to a cap in any three-month period, set as the larger of two measures listed next.

Rule 144
• 1% of the number of shares of our capital stock then outstanding, which will equal shares immediately after the completion of this offering; or

Rule 144
The first measure is 1% of Anthropic's total outstanding shares, a figure still left blank.

Rule 144
• the average weekly trading volume of our Class A common stock during the four calendar weeks preceding the filing of a notice on Form 144 with respect to that sale.

Rule 144
The second measure is the average weekly trading volume of Class A stock over the four weeks before the insider files a sale notice.

Rule 144
Sales of our Class A common stock made in reliance upon Rule 144 by our affiliates or persons selling shares of our Class A common stock on behalf of our affiliates are also subject to certain manner of sale provisions and notice requirements and to the availability of current public information about us.

Rule 144
Insider sales under Rule 144 must also follow rules on how the sale is made, require a filed notice, and depend on current public information about Anthropic being available.

Rule 701
Rule 701 generally allows a stockholder who purchased shares of our capital stock pursuant to a written compensatory plan or contract and who is not deemed to have been an affiliate of our company during the immediately preceding 90 days to sell these shares in reliance upon Rule 144, but without being required to comply with the public information, holding period, volume limitation, or notice provisions of Rule 144. Rule 701 also permits affiliates of our company to sell their Rule 701 shares under Rule 144 without complying with the holding period requirements of Rule 144. All holders of Rule 701 shares, however, are required to wait until 90 days after the date of this prospectus before selling those shares pursuant to Rule 701.

Rule 701
Employees and others who got shares through compensation plans can sell them under Rule 701 with fewer Rule 144 conditions, but all must wait at least 90 days after the IPO.

Distributions
Payments to shareholders count as taxable dividends only to the extent of Anthropic's tax-measured profits; anything beyond that first lowers the investor's cost basis and then counts as gain on a sale.

In order to facilitate the offering of our Class A common stock, Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC, acting as stabilization agent on behalf of the underwriters, may engage in transactions that stabilize, maintain, or otherwise affect the price of our Class A common stock. Specifically, the underwriter may sell more shares of Class A common stock than the underwriters are obligated to purchase under the underwriting agreement, creating a short position. A short sale is covered if the short position is no greater than the number of shares available for purchase under the over-allotment option. The underwriter can close out a covered short sale by exercising the over-allotment option or purchasing shares in the open market. In determining the source of shares to close out a covered short sale, the underwriter will consider, among other things, the open market price of our Class A common stock compared to the price available under the over-allotment option.

The underwriter may also sell shares of Class A common stock in excess of the over-allotment option, creating a naked short position. The underwriter must close out any naked short position by purchasing shares of Class A common stock in the open market. A naked short position is more likely to be created if the underwriter is concerned that there may be downward pressure on the price of our Class A common stock in the open market after pricing that could adversely affect investors who purchase shares of Class A common stock in this offering.

Other Concentrations
Prior to 2026, the Company obtained substantially all of its compute infrastructure from three cloud service providers (“CSPs”). During the six months ended June 30, 2026 (unaudited), the Company obtained a substantial majority of its compute infrastructure from a limited number of CSPs and other suppliers under long-term hosting and lease agreements. This created dependencies and potential vulnerabilities, in that a disruption affecting these counterparties could have adversely affected the Company’s operations. While the Company is expanding its relationships with its existing CSPs, it is also expanding its compute capacity through commitments with additional CSPs and through compute procured from other sources, including leased infrastructure operated on its behalf.

Other Concentrations
Anthropic relies on a handful of cloud providers and other suppliers for compute, the specialized data center chips that train and run Claude; before 2026 three cloud providers such as Amazon, Google or Microsoft supplied nearly all of it, so a disruption at any of them could hurt operations, and it is now adding more suppliers.

Other Concentrations
The Company also provides access to its intelligence service through CSP marketplaces, with CSPs acting as collection agents for the Company in these transactions. During the years ended December 31, 2023, 2024, and 2025, revenue generated from sales through CSP marketplaces to customers represented approximately 11%, 32%, and 47% of total revenue, respectively. During the six months ended June 30, 2025 and 2026 (unaudited), revenue generated from sales through CSP marketplaces to customers represented approximately 44% and 48% of total revenue, respectively. As of December 31, 2024 and 2025 and June 30, 2026 (unaudited), net accounts receivable from sales through CSP marketplaces to customers represented 42%, 60%, and 58% of the Company’s net accounts receivable, respectively.

Sales of Claude through cloud provider marketplaces grew from about 11% of revenue in 2023 to 47% in 2025 and 48% in the first half of 2026, and these providers owed 58% of Anthropic's receivables at June 30, 2026, making them central to both supply and sales.

Fair Value Measurements and Financial Instruments
Fair value is defined as the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. In accordance with Accounting Standards Codification (“ASC”) 820, Fair Value Measurement (“ASC 820”), the Company uses the fair value hierarchy, which prioritizes the inputs used to measure fair value. The hierarchy, as defined below, gives the highest priority to unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities and the lowest priority to unobservable inputs. The three levels of the fair value hierarchy are set forth below:

Fair Value Measurements and Financial Instruments
Fair value is the price an asset would fetch in a normal sale, and accounting rules rank how reliably it is measured into three levels, from market prices down to internal estimates.

Fair Value Measurements and Financial Instruments
Level 1: Observable inputs such as quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities.

Fair Value Measurements and Financial Instruments
Level 1 values come directly from quoted prices for the same asset in active markets, the most reliable kind.

Fair Value Measurements and Financial Instruments
Level 2: Observable inputs other than Level 1 prices such as quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities in active markets, quoted prices in markets that are not active or inputs other than the quoted prices that are observable either directly or indirectly for the full term of the assets or liabilities.

Evaluation of Long-Lived Assets for Impairment
Long-lived assets, such as property and equipment, right-of-use (“ROU”) assets, and finite-lived intangible assets subject to amortization, are reviewed for impairment whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amount of an asset or asset group (collectively, the “asset group”) may not be recoverable. Recoverability of asset groups to be held and used is measured by comparing the carrying amount to the estimated undiscounted future cash flows expected to be generated. If the carrying amount exceeds the undiscounted cash flows, the asset groups are determined to be impaired, and an impairment charge is recognized as the amount by which the carrying amount exceeds its fair value.

Goodwill
Goodwill represents the excess of the purchase price in a business combination over the fair value of net tangible and intangible assets acquired. Goodwill is not subject to amortization but is tested for impairment on an annual basis, performed in the fourth quarter of each year, or whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate the carrying value of the reporting unit may be in excess of the reporting unit’s fair value.

Goodwill is tested for impairment at the reporting unit level by first assessing the qualitative factors to determine whether it is more likely than not that the fair value of the Company’s single reporting unit is less than its carrying amount. Qualitative indicators assessed include consideration of macroeconomic, industry, and market conditions, the Company’s overall financial performance, and personnel or strategy changes. Based on the qualitative assessment, if the Company determines that it is more likely than not that the Company’s single reporting unit’s fair value is less than its carrying amount, a quantitative analysis is performed by comparing the fair value of the Company’s single reporting unit to its carrying value. If the carrying amount of the reporting unit exceeds its fair value, an impairment loss is recognized in an amount equal to that excess, limited to the total amount of goodwill allocated to the reporting unit.

Income Taxes
The Company uses the asset and liability method to account for income taxes. Current income tax expense or benefit represents the amount of income taxes expected to be payable or refundable for the current year. Under this method, deferred income tax assets and liabilities are determined based on differences between the financial statement reporting and tax bases of assets and liabilities and net operating loss and credit carryforwards. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured using enacted tax rates applied to taxable income in the years in which those temporary differences are expected to be recovered or settled. Valuation allowances are established when necessary to reduce deferred tax assets to the amounts that are more-likelythan-not expected to be realized based on the weighting of positive and negative evidence.

Income Taxes
Future realization of deferred tax assets ultimately depends on the existence of sufficient taxable income of the appropriate character (for example, ordinary income or capital gain) within the carryback or carryforward periods available under the applicable tax law. The Company regularly reviews the deferred tax assets for recoverability based on historical taxable income, projected future taxable income, the expected timing of the reversals of existing temporary differences and tax planning strategies. The Company’s judgment regarding future profitability may change due to many factors, including future market conditions and the ability to successfully execute the business plans and/or tax planning strategies. Should there be a change in the ability to recover deferred tax assets, the Company’s income tax provision would increase or decrease in the period in which the assessment is changed.

The Company treats Net CFC Tested Income (formerly referred to as Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income or “GILTI”) as a period cost.

Income Taxes
Anthropic records future tax benefits and costs from timing differences and past losses, but holds back benefits it may not use, so its tax figures depend on judgments about future profits.

Income Taxes
The Company accounts for uncertain tax positions in accordance with ASC 740-10, Accounting for Uncertainty in Income Taxes. The Company recognizes the tax effects of an uncertain tax position only if such position is more likely than not to be sustained based solely on its technical merits as of the reporting date and only in an amount more likely than not to be sustained upon review by the tax authorities. The Company recognizes accrued interest and penalties related to unrecognized tax benefits in the provision for income taxes in the consolidated statements of operations.

Income Taxes
Anthropic counts a tax position only if it would likely survive a tax authority review, and records related interest and penalties as tax expense.

Net Loss per Share
Basic and diluted net loss per share attributable to common stockholders is computed in conformity with the two-class method required for participating securities. The two-class method requires income available to common stockholders for the period to be allocated between common stock and participating securities based upon their respective rights to receive dividends as if all income for the period had been distributed.

Net Loss per Share
Anthropic calculates loss per share by splitting results between common stock and preferred stock according to each class's right to dividends, as if all earnings for the period had been paid out.

Net Loss per Share
The Company considers all series of its redeemable convertible preferred stock to be participating securities as the holders of such stock have the right to participate on a pari passu basis in any distributions to common stockholders.

Net Loss per Share
Anthropic treats every series of its preferred stock as sharing in payouts, because those holders receive any distributions to common stockholders on equal terms.

Net Loss per Share
The holders of the redeemable convertible preferred stock would be entitled to dividends in preference to common stockholders, at specified rates, if declared. Any remaining dividend amounts would then be distributed to the holders of common stock, restricted common stock, and the holders of the redeemable convertible preferred stock on a pro-rata basis assuming conversion of all redeemable convertible preferred stock into common stock. These participating securities do not contractually require the holders of such shares to participate in the Company’s losses. As such, net losses for the periods presented were not allocated to the Company’s participating securities.

Net Loss per Share
Preferred holders would get declared dividends first, but they are not required to absorb losses, so all of Anthropic's net losses are assigned to common stockholders.

Net Loss per Share
Basic net loss per share is computed by dividing the net loss attributable to common stockholders by the weighted-average number of shares of common stock outstanding during the period, less shares subject to repurchase. The diluted net loss per share is computed by giving effect to all potentially dilutive securities outstanding for the period using the treasury stock method or the if-converted method if the effect is dilutive. For periods in which the Company reports net losses, diluted net loss per share is the same as basic net loss per share, because all potentially dilutive securities are anti-dilutive.

Net Loss per Share
Loss per share divides the loss by the average number of common shares; because Anthropic is losing money, counting options and convertible securities would shrink the loss per share, so basic and diluted figures are identical.

This model takes into account the contract terms as well as multiple inputs, such as the Company’s redeemable convertible preferred stock price, risk free interest rates, and expected volatility, some of which the Company could not corroborate with observable market data. The assumptions used in valuing the SAFE liability upon conversion on December 31, 2023 and on January 30, 2024, include volatility, risk free interest rate, and term to liquidity. The Company determined that the SAFEs are not legal form debt (i.e., no creditors’ rights). Fair Value Option
The Company elected to account for the SAFEs and the convertible notes using the fair value option pursuant to ASC 825 and changes in fair value related to the SAFEs and convertible notes are recorded in change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in the Company’s consolidated statements of operations (Note 4). The Company elected to account for the convertible notes using the fair value option pursuant to ASC 825 to eliminate the accounting complexity that would otherwise result from separately accounting for the liability and equity components of the convertible notes under the traditional bifurcation model.

Fair Value Option
Anthropic values its SAFEs and convertible notes at estimated current market value each period, and the changes flow into reported results. It chose this method to avoid splitting each note into separate debt and equity pieces.

Fair Value Option
The estimated fair value of the convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs is determined by using a scenario-based analysis that estimated the fair value of the convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs based on the probability-weighted present value of expected future investment returns, considering possible outcomes available to the SAFE and convertible note holder, including conversions to redeemable convertible preferred stock, Class N common stock and maturity. Issuance costs were expensed as incurred and are reflected in other income (expense), net in the consolidated statements of operations. Changes in fair value of the SAFEs and convertible notes and accrued interest are recorded as change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in the consolidated statements of operations.

Fair Value Option
Anthropic estimates the notes' value by weighting the possible outcomes by how likely each is: conversion into preferred shares, conversion into Class N shares, or repayment at maturity. The resulting value changes are reported in the income statement.

Restricted Stock Units
The Company grants RSUs to employees and the RSUs vest upon the satisfaction of both a service condition and a performance condition. The service condition for these awards is generally satisfied over a four-year vesting period. The performance condition is satisfied upon the occurrence of an “initial event” which is defined as either (i) a qualifying change in control of the Company or (ii) a listing of the Company’s equity securities on an established securities market (including through a traditional public offering, direct listing, or business combination with a special purpose acquisition company), in each case, on or before the seventh anniversary of the grant date, as further defined in such RSU agreements. If the performance condition is not satisfied within seven years of the grant date, all unvested RSUs are forfeited.
